On gb300 it applies only where the MoE backend is Marlin W4A16 (the Kimi-K3 preview build FPM measured), not to stock v0.31.0 gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8 h200 assumed the BF16 envelope: an upper bound on the asymptote; the knee is not a bound no dense Marlin sweep exists on any part host_gather_rate_uva h200 assumed 57,764 B/µs: the PCIe 5.0 raw rate × 128/130 line code × 264/288 no host-gather measurement exists

On H100 the same six entries ship, each fitted from H100's own rows. H100 SXM is the same GH100 die and SM90 kernels as H200 with 0.70× its HBM (3.35 against 4.8 TB/s), and AISimulate's h100_sxm carries the same three tables. The writers fit every part they list from that part's sweep, catalog descriptor and committed siblings; no h200 number enters an h100 entry.

entry h100 value h200 value fit attention_decode_rate_sparse_mla 1,105,500 B/µs (0.330 of peak), floor inherited (14.5 µs) 1,123,200 (0.234) 1.198x, signed 1.057, n = 207; held out ≥ 5 blocks 1.175x (signed 0.853, n = 16); at 10 blocks 1.069x (n = 4) attention_decode_floor_block_index_scores 4.9 µs 4.3 1.086x, n = 414; 246 floor-dominated points 1.067x; per checkpoint 4.95 / 4.90 attention_decode_rate_block_index_scores 2,680,000 B/µs, BwPeak × hbm_derate (3.35 × 0.8) 3,840,000 assumed; the sweep's slope is 6.44 TB/s-equivalent, 1.92× H100's peak gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w4a16_mxfp4_grouped 0.282 / 15 0.245 / 26 1.140x, signed 1.039, n = 27; int4 holdout 1.161x, signed 1.068 gemm_{eps_max,m_half}_w8a16_mxfp8 1.0 / 170, H100's BF16 envelope 0.992 / 110 assumed host_gather_rate_uva 57,764 B/µs, H100's own host_link_bandwidth × 128/130 × 264/288 57,764 assumed

Neither fitted pair scales with bandwidth, and the rows say so directly. On the 207 FlashMLA rows both parts measure, H100 latency is a median 1.05× H200's (1.13× over the slowest tenth), where an HBM-bound read would be 1.43×; on the 27 Marlin token counts it is 0.98–1.06×. So the sparse rate is close to H200's (0.98×) and a larger fraction of H100's peak: at reads of at most 10 blocks per request it is a cost per byte, not a bandwidth, and must not be rescaled between parts by BwPeak. The Marlin ramp differs from H200's because its memory half is charged at H100's lower BwPeak × hbm_derate, and the SM half carries what is left; the pair holds only with that part's own memory half. The sparse rate's batch bias has the same shape on H100 (signed 1.02 at batch 1, 1.44 at 128, 0.59 at 1,024), and the per-request and occupancy forms again leave it (1.186x, 1.179x). The pinned 14.5 µs floor over-prices batch-1 one-block reads (10.1–10.6 µs) by 37–44%.

No end-to-end check is possible on H100. No forward-pass dataset carries DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on h100 under any engine, and the h200 rows FPM does carry are SGLang (next paragraph), so nothing arbitrates the h100 entries either; each rationale says so.

The sparse rate's error depends on batch, and V4.1 runs where the table has no rows. The overall 1.182x hides a batch-dependent bias. Signed, predicted over measured, by batch:

batch 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 512 1024 signed 0.99 1.04 1.07 1.09 1.08 1.05 1.25 1.45 1.10 0.80 0.65
  • Not a missing term this form can carry. A per-request term, floor + c · batch + bytes / rate (1.179x), and an occupancy form, floor + a · ceil(batch · blocks / P) with P fitted at 64 (1.173x), leave the same pattern, so it is batch-dependent scheduling inside the call. The writer fits and prints both.
  • Inside the measured range on the block axis only. V4.1 reads at most 640 tokens per query, 10 FlashMLA blocks (2 window + 8 top-k), inside the 1–130 the table covers. But the sweep's batch × context ≤ 1 M grid pairs 10 blocks only with batch ≤ 8, while V4.1 reads 10 blocks at any context past about 1k tokens, at whatever batch it serves. Above batch 8 the rate's error is what the table says about neighbouring cells: at batch 64 and up, 10–45% slow or 20–35% fast.
  • The holdout is in the small-batch region too. Trained on requests of at most 3 blocks and tested on 5 or more, it predicts 1.210x, signed 0.83 — but all 16 held-out rows are at batch ≤ 16.

The pinned floor over-prices the shortest reads. The floor is this part's 13.5 µs part-wide attention floor, which the kernel inherits for a kind with a rate and no floor. Batch-1 rows of at most one block measure 9.8–11.8 µs, so pinning costs 14–38% there. A free floor lands at 13.3 µs (1.181x against 1.182x) only because a linear form cannot follow the step between one and two blocks. On V4.1 a read of one block occurs on the window-only layers (0, 1, and the DSpark drafts) at contexts up to 64 tokens, and on a ratio-2 layer at context 1, where the indexer emits min((pos + 1) // ratio, topk) = 0 compressed tokens; past that every compressed layer reads at least two blocks.

Why a sparse rate ships for V4.1 when §10.3 withdrew one for V4-Pro. The withdrawn rate was fitted on Pro's 128-head rows — the h128 instance, which Pro runs only below TP 2, since FlashMLA pads n_local_heads — and was to be charged against the kernel's selection rule for Pro's csa4 layers: up to 262,912 tokens at a 1 M context, outside every measured row on the block axis (vLLM itself reads far less there; blis-latency-kernel#32). Every V4.1 sparse read is on the h64 instance at every TP width and inside the block axis. The entry is scoped to this model, so no other deployment moves.

Why the indexer's rate is assumed when its floor is measured. The collector gives every query row one block table, so the unique key footprint is at most 34.6 MB, and the fitted throughput, 5.35 TB/s-equivalent, exceeds the 4.8 TB/s HBM peak — impossible from HBM, and consistent with the shared keys being served from cache. A fit of that slope would be clean and wrong in the §3 sense. The floor is a launch cost: the 238 points whose work term is under 5% of it identify it at 1.050x, and each checkpoint alone gives 4.29 and 4.28 µs. In serving each request's keys are its own, read at ceil(context / ratio) × 132 B; V4.1's ratios are 1 and 2, so the scan grows with context while the attention it feeds does not. The committed rate is NVIDIA's empirical HBM fraction (BwPeak × hbm_derate), not a bound: the real rate cannot exceed BwPeak, so it can be pessimistic by at most 1.25x (scan time over-priced), while how optimistic it can be is not bounded. The writer refuses to keep assuming it if a future sweep's throughput stops exceeding the HBM peak.

Why the Marlin ramp is fitted in the kernel's composition, and what it is coupled to. A weight-only GEMM is two costs, a BF16 mma.sync compute and a narrow weight read. The kernel sums them for the routed term, and fitting the ramp as what remains after the kernel's own memory half is the only way it composes back to the measurement. That couples it to blis-latency-kernel's routed term as #44 (483f6aa) implements it:

  • compute and memory summed, the ramp evaluated at the step's token count, compute at the BF16 peak, memory as ExpertsTouched experts' stored bytes at BwPeak × hbm_derate, imbalance and SM derate 1;
  • FLOPs the rank's own, the intermediate width divided by tp, which #44 applies on this ramp;
  • no Marlin padding: #44 also scales routed FLOPs and bytes by Marlin's round-up of inter / tp to a multiple of 128 (V4.1 at TP8: 288 → 384). Fitted at tp 1, where that pad is 1, the fit has not checked it; it is the consumer's addition;
  • stored bytes per weight as blis-schemas v0.3.0's StoredBytes gives them for MXFP4, 0.5 + 1/32, which #44 charges. At payload-only bytes (0.5, what kernel main e9cf217 charges) the fit would be 0.240 / 28 on h200, 0.114 / 58 on gb300.

A change to any of those — sum versus max, the ramp's argument, the byte count — needs a refit. The fit holds out on vLLM's int4 Marlin MoE, a different geometry and weight type: 1.196x on h200 and 1.266x on gb300. Its error grows with expert and tensor parallelism; the committed BF16 ramp does the same on BF16 Triton experts (on h200, 2.83x at ep 8 and 8.33x at ep 32, printed by the writer's form check), so that growth is a property of the routed-term form — though #48144 above means the 0.25.0 ep > 1 rows may not be v0.31.0's.

For scale: kernel main prices MXFP4 experts on H200 at the FP8 peak with the FP8 ramp. That is 1,456 TFLOPS effective where Marlin sustains about 242.

What does not ship, and why.

  • A ramp for CutlassExpertsMxfp4, what stock v0.31.0 runs for compressed-tensors MXFP4 experts on Blackwell. AISimulate carries no such rows on any Blackwell part.
  • Prefill pairs for either kernel. No kernel-level table carries V4.1's prefill path (flash_mla_sparse_fwd over a gathered compressed region, fp8_fp4_mqa_logits), and the kernel has no per-kind prefill name to read one with.
  • SGLang's dsv41_module_perf (h200). It is eager, a module timing (MQALayer.forward with projections), at batch ≤ 3 and context ≤ 2,049, and flat at 0.8–2.0 ms. That is launch-bound, not a kernel rate.

No end-to-end check exists for vLLM, and that is stated rather than waived. At FPM revision 03e006de, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on h200, b200, b300, gb200 and gb300 is measured under SGLang only -- another engine, another MoE kernel (w4a16_mxfp4_humming on h200) and another checkpoint revision (fb2764a5 against the catalog's 52544481). The only vLLM V4.1 leaf is a historical GB200 dev build labelled "comparator". So FPM cannot be the arbiter §3 requires for V4.1's vLLM pricing; an earlier version of this section said it could. blis-registry#42 stays open with no arbiter until a vLLM V4.1 forward-pass measurement exists. Separately, blis-latency-kernel main cannot price the model: it refuses the fp8_ds_mla cache (#36), charges 20,480 KV bytes per token against roughly 1,790 (#30), drops the 128-token window from the sparse read (#32) and does not pad FlashMLA's heads (#39). blis-latency-kernel#44 closes all four. Three consumer-contract points go with the entries, each stated in them:

  • Multi-token decode. The sparse rate was fitted at one query token per request. Under DSpark speculation a request decodes 1 + num_spec_tokens query tokens, and FlashMLA treats each as its own query; how much of that read the tokens of one request share is unmeasured. #44 charges the read per query row and records that as an assumption (sparse_read_per_query), which is what this entry asks of a consumer.
  • Routed FLOPs under pure TP. This ramp's FLOPs are each rank's own (inter / tp). #44 divides routed FLOPs by tp on the weight-only Marlin ramps, as this fit requires, and keeps its documented over-charge on the native ramps, where it cancels a measured error; blis-latency-kernel#47 tracks removing it there. A consumer that charged this ramp the whole expert would price its compute half tp times too slow.
  • gb300's Marlin ramp stays unread while ramps are chosen by format and chip, which on gb300 is the FP4 class — right for stock v0.31.0. It is for scoring the Kimi-K3 preview build's FPM run, for blis-registry#41 (the Kimi-K3/GB300 FPM check of the KDA pair).

Every V4.1 attention read in blis-catalog 0.3.0 is sparse_mla, the window-only layers (0, 1, and the DSpark drafts at a 133-token window) included, all inside the block axis above.

docs.title: 10.6 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash prefill attention, prefill indexer, mHC and host terms
docs.text:
Before these entries the kernel priced three V4.1 operators with numbers fitted on a different kernel or with none: the sparse-MLA PREFILL attention and the indexer's prefill logits with the generic full-attention prefill pair (attention_prefill_floor / attention_prefill_work_scale, fitted on context_attention_perf), and mHC as Elementwise bytes at the HBM rate with no floor -- 0.07 ms a one-token decode step against 1.05 ms measured, one of the two terms behind V4.1's 19-30% fast low-load ITL. Every number below is written by scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_prefill.py or scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_host.py, both with --check; each part is fitted from its own rows. The per-call forms are stated in each entry's rationale.

entry (scope: h200 / h100, deepseek-v4.1-flash) method h200 h100 fit (h200) attention_prefill_{floor,per_request,per_token,rate}_sparse_mla measured 14.8 µs, 1.323 µs, 0.049 µs, 3,159,685 B/µs 15.5, 1.325, 0.0571, 3,509,505 1.067x, signed 1.003, n = 1,642 (not V4.1's operating point: signed 0.81 at 10 blocks); held out on blocks 1.137x (signed 0.91), on chunk length 1.036x attention_prefill_{floor,per_token,rate}_block_index_scores assumed (proxy kernel) 4.1 µs, 0.00466 µs, 7,298,637 B/µs 4.7, 0.00441, 7,364,876 1.066x, signed 0.969, n = 3,504; held out on context 1.054x, on rows 1.142x mhc_{floor,rate}_pre measured 8.9 µs, 1,799,384 B/µs 9.3, 1,325,488 1.052x, n = 70; across hidden 1.103x / 1.073x mhc_{floor,rate}_post measured 3.0 µs, 1,850,611 B/µs 3.1, 1,306,352 1.091x, n = 70; across hidden 1.178x / 1.109x

Sparse-MLA prefill is fitted on the kernel table's prefill rows, in four terms. dsv4_hca_attn_module_perf times forward_mqa alone; its isl > 1 rows run the prefill branch (SWA and compressed gather, index combine, flash_mla_sparse_fwd). A floor plus a work rate over the decode fit's block-and-record count gives 1.390x with a strong batch bias (signed 0.15 at batch 1,024); a per-request and a per-query-token term remove it (1.067x, every batch within 0.96-1.05 signed). The per-token term, 0.049 µs, is the cost of a query's own traffic -- 64 padded heads of 512 BF16 in and out -- at about the part's empirical HBM rate. The fit uses only rows reading at most V4.1's 10 blocks a query. Its weak point is V4.1's operating point: the only 10-block rows are short chunks at step 65,536, under-priced 1.31x (signed 0.81), and long chunks at 10 blocks are not in the table; long-chunk rows at 11-67 blocks extrapolate at 1.05x. So the 1.067x headline is not V4.1's error. It is dominated by the rows V4.1 does not run: 980 of the 1,642 rows are at 3 blocks, 20 at 10 and none at 8-9. At V4.1's read the evidence is signed 0.81 in sample (under-priced) and, trained on fewer blocks, signed 0.91 held out on 7-10 blocks; the honest statement of this entry's error at V4.1's operating point is "about 10-20% fast, from 71 rows", not 1.067x.

These entries ship without the end-to-end check §3 and the evidence page ask for, as an explicit exception. No vLLM forward-pass measurement of V4.1 exists on any part (§10.5: FPM's V4.1 rows are SGLang), so the rule cannot be met by waiting for the data on hand; the alternative is to keep pricing V4.1 with entries fitted on other kernels, which is the known larger error. Each entry therefore says it has no arbiter, and blis-registry#42 stays open until a vLLM V4.1 forward-pass measurement exists. The SM90 sparse prefill device code is unchanged between the FlashMLA pins of vLLM 0.25.0 and 0.31.0 (renames only). V4.1's ratio-1/2 layers gather their whole compressed stream before the kernel; the ratio-128 rows hold that gather only at 1/128 of the context, so it stays with the catalog's prefill_dequant_gather node.

The indexer's prefill is a proxy, and is labelled so. vLLM v0.31.0's prefill indexer runs DeepGEMM's ragged fp8_fp4_mqa_logits; the entries are fitted on the paged fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits at prefill shapes. Unlike decode, the sweep's shared block table is representative here (every query row of a request reads the same keys), and the fitted throughput is compute-like (906 TFLOPS at 64 heads). The 32-head V4.1 indexer is scaled linearly from 64, an assumption. The ragged kernel is measured, on another lane: SGLang 0.5.14's glm5_mqa_logits_module_perf times deep_gemm.fp8_mqa_logits at GLM-5's indexer geometry -- 32 index heads x 128, FP8 keys, ratio 1, V4.1's head count. Evaluated as the kernel charges it, the proxy is 1.50x there, signed 0.93 (h200) and 0.90 (h100); signed 0.89 / 0.82 on long chunks over long prefixes and 1.18 / 1.09 at V4.1's 8,192-token chunk. An earlier review read the table's num_heads (GLM-5's 64 attention heads) as index heads and found the proxy over-pricing by 1.4-1.7x; at the config's 32 it does not. The ragged rows are not fitted because the lane decision is open: SGLang 0.5.14 calls upstream DeepGEMM's fp8_mqa_logits, vLLM v0.31.0 its fork's fp8_fp4_mqa_logits on the FP8 path, and the two pins' device code has not been compared. fit_deepseek_v41_prefill.py prints the comparison and each rationale states it.

mHC is measured per site and interpolated by bytes. mhc_module_perf times TileLang mhc_pre and mhc_post (two sites a row) at hidden 4096 and 7168; W = tokens x hidden x 8 B carries the hidden size, so one floor and rate per component fit both, and each hidden size predicted from the other lands within 1.06-1.18x. The pre includes the TF32 prenorm GEMM, so the catalog's hc_*_fn GEMM must not also be charged. On SM90 v0.31.0 runs the fused delayed post+pre, which above 32 tokens is the same two kernels and at <= 32 folds the post into the GEMM -- so at decode sizes the pair is an upper bound by about one launch.

Two terms were looked for and do not ship. Routed MoE at V4.1's geometry: no vLLM collection holds a hidden 5120 / inter 2304 / 384-expert / top-6 W4A16 row on h200 or h100. The only rows at that geometry are SGLang dev-1aa0e962 (flashinfer_cutlass at moe_tp 2, mxfp4_humming at moe_tp 4, ep 1, 15 token counts each) -- other kernels and another sharding than vLLM v0.31.0's Marlin at EP8 -- so the Kimi-K3-geometry Marlin ramp stays, with its evidence class. The compressor: no table isolates it; the csa/hca context-module tables time the whole attention module, projections included, and a residual from them would be a module-derived term of the kind §10.1 rejects. It stays at the catalog's bytes.

Host terms. host_launch_eager_per_kernel (92.87 µs, assumed) is V4.1's per-launch Python dispatch in an eager (cudagraph NONE) step -- vLLM v0.31.0 cannot torch.compile this model, so NONE is plain eager PyTorch. It is backed out of an internal enforce-eager H200 serving run of the same model (ITL flat at 93.8-101.6 ms from c1 to c64). The run's report is not redistributed: validator/testdata/anchors/v41_h200_enforce_eager_anchor.json holds only what the fit needs -- the plateau's levels, median, minimum and maximum ITL, the setup and the report's sha256 -- and --check re-derives it from a local copy of the report when V41_EAGER_ANCHOR_REPORT names one, and checks its internal consistency otherwise. The division is by the KERNEL's own launch count and device time for that step, a recorded input: v41_kernel_eager_basis.json, written by --record-device from diagnosis/kdevice (public kernel API) with clean kernel, registry and catalog commits. --check refuses a basis recorded for another anchor, scenario, host composition or step type: the anchor is a decode step, so the count must be the decode-only 972 (a step with a prefill row also launches the graph's 46 phase: prefill gathers, 1,018; kernel 993ddeb used 1,018 on every step, which gave 89.4 µs). The composition is additive, as the kernel's is: step = launches x (eager + dispatch) + device, so e = (ITL - device) / launches - host_launch_per_kernel = (96.56 - 3.18 ms) / 972 - 3.2 µs = 92.87 µs. A launch-overlap form, step ~ max(launches, device) (vLLM enqueues eager kernels asynchronously), was tried in the kernel and gave 96.14 µs here, and was REJECTED: it does not reproduce the H200 DSpark arm's capture-ceiling collapse at c32, whose measured throughput the additive form matches (blis-latency-kernel 07ed424, TestTheEagerDecodeAnchorIsAdditive, which pins the constant at 92.75-93.7 µs). The basis records the composition and --check refuses any other. The committed basis is kernel 07ed424 (972 launches, 3.18 ms with the mHC entries). The constant is valid only with the basis and the composition it was divided by. It is derived on H200 nodes only: the h200 entry is assumed (backed out of the anchor), and the other eight parts, h100 included, carry it as a separate copied entry (copied_from: hardware=h200,...). That copy is an ASSUMPTION about host CPU and driver launch cost, not a derivation; an H100 enforce-eager ITL anchor (same model, TP8, no speculation, c1-c64) would replace it. The host set's coverage rule is checked per name and model across entries, so the split is allowed. host_admission_per_token (2.67 µs, assumed) is a timing of vLLM v0.31.0's own V4.1 front end -- render, tokenize, block hash -- taken on the diagnosis workstation (Apple M1 Max, one Python thread) with synthetic text. No part it is scoped to matches that host, so on every part it is an assumed transfer of the measurement, labelled as the eager copy is; the same timing on the serving node's CPU would replace it. And host_admission_per_request is 0.0, not_charged only because blis-schemas requires that method for a zero value: what was timed has no fixed term above noise, but the bench does not time HTTP handling, validation, the IPC to EngineCore or scheduler admission, so the zero is an inference bounded only end to end (an 8,030-token c1 TTFT of 37.15 ms in total), not a structural zero. These two model-scoped entries sit after their part-wide namesakes in the same set, the one arrangement test_a_model_scoped_entry_never_shadows_a_part_wide_one allows: last-in-file-order and scoped-wins resolve it the same way.

docs.title: 10.7 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode: a two-branch FlashMLA form, and what stays assumed
docs.text:
The single decode rate (§10.5) is 1.18-1.20x with a batch bias it cannot carry: signed 1.45-1.54 at batch 128 and 0.59-0.80 at 1,024. The FlashMLA decode rows show two regimes. At small batch the call is latency-bound and flat in batch to about 128 rows: one block costs about 10.2 µs (h200) / 10.4 µs (h100), any read of two or more blocks adds about 3.5 µs at once (the split-KV combine launch), then 0.2-0.3 µs a block. At large batch it is linear in rows through the origin: one cost per query row and one per block read. So scripts/fit_deepseek_v41_decode.py fits, per part, on the rows of at most V4.1's 10 blocks:

t = max(launch_floor + split_floor x [B > 1] + B x 37,376 B / serial_rate,
        sum over query rows (per_token + blocks x 37,376 B / throughput_rate))
part launch floor split serial rate per token throughput rate fit held out rows ≤ 256 → ≥ 512 held out blocks ≤ 4 → ≥ 6 h200 10.0 µs 3.1 µs 115,005 B/µs 0.05437 µs 1.30 TB/s 1.061x (single rate 1.176x) 1.038x (single rate 1.375x) 1.059x h100 10.3 µs 3.6 µs 145,351 B/µs 0.06567 µs 1.27 TB/s 1.060x (single rate 1.193x) 1.028x (single rate 1.502x) 1.058x

The per-token term lands near the prefill fit's own (0.049 / 0.057 µs), an independent check that it is each row's query and output traffic. The weakness is stated in each entry: the throughput branch is identified only by the batch ≥ 256 rows, which are at 1-3 blocks. Trained on rows ≤ 64 the form predicts ≥ 128 at 1.8-1.9x, worse than the single rate (1.3x), because no training row reaches that branch. At 10 blocks the throughput branch binds above about 47 query rows per rank, a region the sweep's batch x context ≤ 1M grid never measures; there the per-block cost is extrapolated from 1-3 blocks, as the single rate's is. Batches 16-64 at 4+ blocks are under-priced (signed 0.83-0.93).

The names are new. attention_decode_floor_sparse_mla is deliberately not used: the kernel reads that name today as the floor of the single-rate pair, which was fitted over the inherited part-wide floor, and would silently re-price it. The kernel uses the form only when all five resolve.

What stays assumed, and why.

  • The indexer's decode scan rate (attention_decode_rate_block_index_scores). Both kernel-level sweeps of fp8_fp4_paged_mqa_logits -- vLLM 0.24.0/0.25.0 and SGLang 0.5.14 -- give every query row one shared block table, and none flushes L2. The largest unique footprint, one request at a 1M context, is 34.6 MB, inside the 50 MB L2, and its implied throughput is 7.2 TB/s-equivalent on h100 (above the 3.35 TB/s HBM peak) even at batch 1. No row reads its keys from HBM, so no row identifies the HBM-bound scan V4.1 runs in serving, where it is the one decode term that grows with context (ratio 1 and 2 over all 40 layers' index sources). Its per-row term is identified (about 0.006-0.01 µs a row at 64 heads, past 256 rows) but is under 3 µs a layer at V4.1's batches and is not shipped.
  • The decode top-k. vLLM v0.31.0 runs cooperative_topk up to 64 rows and persistent_topk beyond (indexer_topk.py, index_topk 512 on SM90). AISimulate times only SGLang's topk_transform_512 (dsv4_csa_topk_calib_perf) and its GLM-5 fused variant, different kernels with mode switches visible in the rows (0 µs, then a 48-85 µs plateau, then ~10 µs past 128k). Nothing measures vLLM's kernels, and the catalog keeps pricing the logits write and top-k read as index_logits_topk bytes.
  • compute_global_topk_indices_and_lens and V4.1's candidate select/mask: unmeasured.
  • Host and launch terms. AISimulate carries no host, launch or graph-replay rows on any part; every operator row is a device timing under CUDA-graph replay. The collective floors on h100 and h200 are already measured (NCCL and vLLM custom all-reduce), so they are not among the assumed terms. The only public timing of an engine's Python path found is FPM's GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM 0.31.0 fidelity pairs on GB300 (next paragraph); nothing times graph replay or eager launch on Hopper.

Held-out evidence for a per-request host term, not used to fit anything. Each of FPM's five GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM 0.31.0 GB300 leaves (FP8 TP2/TP4, NVFP4 TP1/TP2/TP4, checkpoint eb9eb208, FULL_AND_PIECEWISE, async scheduling off) ships source-fidelity.json, pairing each held-out point's FPM step time with a "clean" timer that excludes schedule(), the scheduler-output send and update_from_output. Re-derived here from the five files: an OLS of decode (FPM - clean) on batch over 77 points a leaf gives 20.4, 24.9, 26.4, 27.6 and 32.6 µs per request (intercepts 16-282 µs); the SGLang 0.5.20 control leaf gives -1.2. It does not hold at small batch: fitted on batch ≤ 8 alone the slopes range from -21 to +33 µs, and the residual at batch ≥ 16 is up to 1 ms, so the per-request reading rests on batch 16-32. Caveats: Grace (Arm) hosts, FPM and clean are separate runs, batch ≤ 32, and the clean timer's boundary is described only in words. It is the first in-version public timing of a per-request scheduler cost, and it agrees in magnitude with fit_host_step_per_request.py's form; it is recorded as held-out evidence for that term on gb300 and moves no value.

docs.title: 11. Memory occupancy: what composes, and where each term comes from
docs.text: cost-model-memory.yaml exists because a consumer was carrying three per-rank memory magnitudes as constants in its own source — CUDA-graph capture at 512 MiB, collective buffers at 392 MiB, activation scratch at "a few live buffers" (×4) — where no provenance readout could see them (inference-sim/blis-registry#33). They set how many sequences fit, so they are not soft numbers.

docs.title: 11.1 The composition, taken from NVIDIA's capacity path
docs.text:
AISimulate's KV-capacity estimate (aisimulate_core/sdk/memory.py) charges, per rank and outside the KV budget:

weights + activation + nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank + engine_workspace_bytes
        + cudagraph_capture_bytes_<mode>

Every term adds. Two questions the consumer could not answer from its side are settled by the source rather than by preference:

  • nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank is the whole collective-buffer reservation. base_backend.py sums nccl_mem and other_mem; neither contains the other.
  • engine_workspace_bytes (misc.other_mem) does not include CUDA-graph capture. This registry's own rationale previously said it did; AISimulate annotates other_mem as "excludes CUDA graph reservation" (support/config_profile.py) and takes the graph reservation as a separate argument (capacity.py, cuda_graph_reserved_bytes). Adding a capture term on top therefore does not double-count. The rationale is corrected in emit_primitives.py and in all nine committed entries.

docs.title: 11.2 Activation scratch — vendor_spec, NVIDIA's table
docs.text:
activation = max(activation_buffer_count_<family>_<N>rank · max_num_batched_tokens · h · 2,
                 activation_scratch_floor_bytes)

The multiple is AISimulate's ACTIVATION_COEFFICIENTS, which the vLLM backend reuses from TRT-LLM's; emit_memory.py reads it from the source with ast and refuses if vLLM stops aliasing it. Two rows are registered because the kernel can tell only whether a model routes to experts: dense (the LLAMA row, 11 / 6.5 / 5 / 5 at 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 ranks) and MoE (22 / 13 / 10 / 10). h is num_attention_heads × head_dim, equal to hidden_size unless a config declares a different head_dim; N is min(tp, 8).

Three scoping decisions, each a finding rather than a convenience:

  • The 2 is the model dtype, not the served one. The issue proposed sizing scratch at the served width (1 byte for fp8). vLLM's quantized linears return out_dtype=x.dtype (vllm/model_executor/kernels/linear/scaled_mm/cutlass.py): the fp8 operand is a transient copy, and the residual stream stays bf16. Halving it would understate an fp8 deployment.
  • Not scoped by graph mode. vLLM measures the activation peak in an eager profile run and the capture separately (gpu_worker.py); a mode-scoped multiple would charge capture twice.
  • Not scoped by hardware, because the source states no per-part value; the scope lists every catalog part, under the same coverage test as the host set.

Engine. These are the vLLM figures. SGLang's table is about 1.3× higher with a further 15% overhead, and SGLang does not charge activations inside its static pool. A deployment states no engine identity and the consumer prices vLLM, so no SGLang row is registered.

Not registered: the MoE dispatch workspace. AISimulate adds tokens · h · num_experts · top_k / ep / 128 · 4 bytes for its DeepSeek-derived families and Kimi-K2.5 — 3,758,096,384 bytes for DeepSeek-V3 at 8,192 tokens and ep 1. That is a formula over catalog facts and the fp8 block size, not a learned magnitude, so it belongs to the consumer's composition; it is recorded here so it is not lost.

docs.title: 11.3 CUDA-graph capture — assumed, anchored on vLLM's own measurements
docs.text:
No dataset this project reads measures it. AISimulate takes it from the caller with a zero default; the FPM dataset records each run's cudagraph_mode and capture sizes in its resolved configs but no memory figure (all 417 of its JSON, text and TSV files under 3.5 MB at revision 68fa3add were read), and its SGLang raw evidence was collected with prefill capture off.

vLLM measures it on every start-up and logs it, and users paste those logs into issues. mine_vllm_cudagraph_memory.py collected 506 samples from 677 vLLM issues into docs/vllm-cudagraph-capture-samples.csv, which is committed so the anchor is reproducible offline. The medians on catalog parts are 0.80 GiB for PIECEWISE (n = 18) and 1.08 GiB for FULL_AND_PIECEWISE (n = 22); the replaced constant was 0.50 GiB. The dimension is vLLM's profiler (gpu_model_runner.profile_cudagraph_memory): one first capture per mode, sized by the largest shape, plus at least 1 MiB per further graph, with PIECEWISE and FULL overlaid in one pool. So the cost is dominated by the largest captured shape, not proportional to the number of shapes.

FULL and FULL_DECODE_ONLY have too few samples (one and four logs, only one of them on a catalog part), so they are charged the FULL_AND_PIECEWISE figure as an upper bound — they capture a subset of its graphs into the same pool — with the direction declared. NONE is not_charged at zero.

Why this source is admissible here and nowhere else. §3's separation is about fitting: an uncontrolled sample cannot identify a per-primitive constant. These entries are not fitted and are not measured; they are assumed entries whose magnitude is oriented by the only public record of the quantity, in the pattern host_admission_per_request set. None of the samples is from InferenceX or FPM, and the single-sourcing tests (test_generated_from_aisimulate.py) still govern the primitive and collective sets, which this set is kept out of for exactly that reason.

docs.title: 11.4 What it changes on the issue's fixture
docs.text:
On deepseek-v3-h200-fp8-sglang-tp8 (tp 8, hidden_size 7168, 8,192 batched tokens, PIECEWISE), resolved through blis-latency-kernel's own resolve.Load:

term hardcoded registry activation scratch 469,762,048 (×4) 1,174,405,120 (MoE 8-rank ×10) CUDA-graph capture 536,870,912 858,783,744 collective buffers 411,041,792 411,041,792 (nccl_communicator_bytes_8rank) engine workspace not charged 3,758,096,384 total 1,417,674,752 6,202,327,040

The set is committed ahead of its reader: the kernel reads none of it yet, and inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel#22 is sequenced to land after it.

docs.title: 12. Speculative acceptance profiles
docs.text: acceptance/inferencex-golden-al.yaml holds the acceptance lengths a simulator advances speculating requests by (inference-sim/blis-registry#44), in blis-schemas#65's format. It is not a coefficient set: acceptance does not price a step, it sets how many tokens a step yields. The generated tables and the set's caveats are on the acceptance reference page.

docs.title: 12.1 One source, transcribed
docs.text: Every value comes from SemiAnalysis InferenceX's inferencex-e2e/infx/golden_al_distribution/*.yaml, vendored under validator/testdata/inferencex/ at the commit scripts/emit_acceptance_profiles.py cites. The emitter reads each acceptance length, and every provenance field a file's header states (the source Actions run, benchmark, category, sampling, image, TP and engine settings, including speculative-config: a=b | c=d lines), and types none of them. Every header is read, carried or not: a piece stating a value, as key: value or key=value with any spelling of key, that the emitter does not know how to transcribe fails the run, so a setting cannot be silently dropped. Only named prose lines are exempt. A header that states method: must state the curve's method; one that does not is checked against its "Measured on (..., vLLM )" line. An acceptance length is measured; the one file InferenceX marks provisional is copied, with copied_from naming the measured profile it repeats, and the emitter checks that the two values agree.

docs.title: 12.2 Model names: resolved, or refused
docs.text:
InferenceX keys a curve by the lower-cased basename of the Hugging Face repository it served (MODEL_KEY in its SPEED-Bench collectors). The emitter resolves that key to the catalog model whose source.repo has that basename, against the vendored copy of every catalog model.yaml. A key that resolves to none is not carried, and the set's caveats name it. A quantised checkpoint is a different catalog model, so InferenceX's qwen3.5-397b-a17b-nvfp4 does not become the catalog's bf16 qwen3.5-397b-a17b.

One alias is allowed, with its evidence in the emitter: glm-5.3-fp8, the provisional curve's key, is InferenceX's name for zai-org/GLM-5.3, the catalog's glm-5.3. The emitter fails if the catalog stops recording that repository for it.

docs.title: 12.3 Curves a key cannot tell apart
docs.text: A profile is keyed by model, method, K, thinking mode and category; it cannot state the drafter or the draft sampler. Where InferenceX publishes two curves that differ only in those, at most one can be carried. The emitter follows InferenceX's own resolver (curves.py, curve_name): MiniMax-M3's base EAGLE3 curve is carried and the GQA-drafter variant is not, and neither Kimi-K3 DSpark curve is carried, because the resolver itself refuses to choose between greedy and probabilistic draft sampling. Every file is classified in the emitter's CURVES table, and an unclassified file fails the run.

docs.title: 12.4 Hardware: stated, or read from the run
docs.text:
A measured profile must name the part it was measured on. Most headers state it ("B300, vLLM MTP"). The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash file states none, and its collecting job ran on InferenceX's b200-nscale cluster, launched through the B200 benchmark base, so its profiles say b200. blis-registry#44 describes the curve as measured on B300; the run contradicts that, and the run is what is recorded. The emitter's RUN_HARDWARE table holds each run's runner, read through the GitHub API, and is checked against every header that also states a part. Files that name no engine image say so in engine_image: their runs' logs have expired, so the image cannot be recovered.

The collectors are named <prefix>_fp4_b300_vllm.sh because speedbench-al.yml requires that name and labels every collection PRECISION: fp4; the fp4 is not what they serve. Each serves its checkpoint's own weights, and the DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GLM-5.2 collectors set --kv-cache-dtype fp8, which their profiles record as kv_cache_dtype. The emitter's COLLECTORS table holds what each collector serves, and a curve whose collector it has not read fails the run.

docs.title: 12.5 Gates
docs.text: emit_acceptance_profiles.py --check runs in every CI job (validator/test_acceptance_profiles.py), because its inputs are vendored. The rederive job also checks the vendored curves and catalog models against InferenceX and blis-catalog at their pinned commits, and re-runs the emitter against the upstream checkout. Schema validation is blis-schemas' cmd/validate-registry, which reads acceptance/ from blis-schemas#74 on. CI's schema-validate pins that pull request's head commit for now; a release tag carrying it must replace the commit before this merges.

docs.title: Reproducing every coefficient from the original datasets
docs.text:
This guide takes a reader from two public datasets to the coefficient values this registry ships. It exists because a fitted constant whose fit cannot be re-run is not a measurement, it is a number someone wrote down. Two earlier sets in this registry — the per-GPU roofline-* MFU sets and trained-physics — were removed precisely because they could not be re-derived: trained-physics carried fifteen entries, eleven of them fitted: true, with no sources block on any entry and no fitter in scripts/; the five roofline-* sets carried two method: literature entries each, citing an issue number rather than a dataset. Both are recoverable from git history if ever needed.

For why the coefficients take the forms they do, and for the train/validate separation that governs which dataset may be used for what, read methodology.md first. This document is the mechanical companion: where the data comes from, and which command regenerates which file.

docs.title: AISimulate — per-operator sweeps and system descriptors
docs.text:
Repository https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate Docs https://ai-dynamo.org/aisimulate/ Licence Apache-2.0, with one MIT third-party file carved out in the LICENSE NOTICE and attributed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. GitHub's license API reports NOASSERTION because of that preamble; the text itself says "Except for the third-party material identified in that notice file, this codebase is licensed under the Apache License 2.0", and source files carry SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0. Provenance Successor to ai-dynamo/aiconfigurator; method described in arXiv:2601.06288. Fetch git clone https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate — the sweeps are checked into git as Parquet. Git LFS is needed only for retained legacy .txt assets, which no fit in this registry reads. pip install aisimulate also ships the tree inside the wheel. Pin Every committed value re-derives at 2f0f4cd8606d580567b253d02f3d699fe36db865 (2026-10-10), with blis-catalog at 0.5.0 (b5550f7; the commit validator/testdata/catalog vendors). The rederive CI job checks out both; bump either deliberately, with the diff the writers produce. A catalog revision that changes a part's datasheet figure moves every rate fitted as a fraction of it. Python pip install -r requirements-fit.txt — the validator's dependencies plus numpy, pandas and pyarrow, which the fitters need to read Parquet.

The two trees the fits read are not at the repository root:

python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/<sku>.yaml          # system descriptors
python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data/<sku>/<op>/<framework>/<version>/*.parquet

Export that second path once; every script below honours it:

export AISIMULATE_DATA=<aisimulate>/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data
export BLIS_CATALOG=<path-to-blis-catalog>

Dataset SKU directories are not catalog chip names. The sweeps use h200_sxm, h100_sxm, b200_sxm, b300_sxm, gb200, a100_sxm, l40s; the catalog calls the same parts h200, h100, b200, b300, gb200-nvl72, a100-sxm, l40s. The mapping lives in each fitter's SKUS table and is passed as sku:chip pairs. There is no gb200_nvl72 directory.

Framework lanes present in the data tree are vllm, sglang, trtllm and, for comm, nccl. Which lane is admissible for which operator is a methodology question, not a mechanical one — see the lane table in methodology.md.

docs.title: FPM — whole-forward-pass measurements
docs.text:
Dataset https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/aisimulate-fpm-dataset ("AISimulate FPM Dataset"; FPM = Forward Pass Model) Licence Apache-2.0, same NVIDIA text and MIT carve-out as the code repository Pinning By commit SHA — the dataset has no tags and its history is actively rewritten. Cite a SHA, never main. Fetch huggingface_hub.snapshot_download(repo_id="nvidia/aisimulate-fpm-dataset", repo_type="dataset", revision=<sha>)

Layout is data/<org>--<model>/<system>/<framework>/<version>/<parallelism>/{manifest.json,fpm/,measurements/}. The per-leaf measurement Parquets under measurements/ are what this registry validates against; the three configs the HuggingFace datasets-server exposes (catalog/configurations, fpm/files, measurements/files, 326 rows in total) are file indexes, not measurements — a reader who stops at those will conclude the dataset is three hundred rows.

At the revision this registry validated against, the measurement Parquets hold 85,484 rows, every one backend: vllm, splitting by the KV axis into 12,522 pure decode (total_prefill_tokens == 0), 5,226 pure prefill (total_kv_read_tokens == 0) and 67,736 mixed. Derive these counts rather than quoting them: the dataset is rewritten, and the workload_kind column labels any row carrying prefill tokens as prefill, which is a coarser split than the one fitting needs.

FPM is used for validation and model selection. It may fit only a term that is itself a property of the whole forward pass, never a per-primitive constant, and no committed coefficient cites it. methodology.md §3 gives the argument, including why an earlier, stricter rule was relaxed.

docs.title: 2. What each dataset's units are
docs.text:
Two traps, both of which have produced wrong numbers in this project before:

  • latency in every AISimulate Parquet is MILLISECONDS. Reading it as seconds gives a 1000× error that happens to look plausible on some parts.
  • FPM's total_kv_read_tokens is summed OVER THE BATCH, while the kernel takes a per-request context length. Dividing by batch_size is required.

docs.title: 3. Regenerating each coefficient set
docs.text:
Run from the repository root with AISIMULATE_DATA and BLIS_CATALOG exported. Two sets are fully generated and are compared by diff; the rest are fitted per part, and each printed value should match the committed entry.

Entry counts quoted in this section were taken when each passage was written, and sets have grown since. The current count of every set, by method, is on the reference pages, which are generated from the committed files.

docs.title: cost-model-primitives.yaml — per-family writers
docs.text:
No single command regenerates this set; each family has an owner (table below), and emit_primitives.py owns only the vendor_spec descriptor entries. Those it reads from AISimulate's own systems/<sku>.yaml — the keys are mem_bw_empirical_scaling_factor, pcie_bw, misc.nccl_mem (the rank-count→bytes map) and misc.other_mem, several of which NVIDIA annotates in-file as "nonofficial correction based on observations". It takes the systems directory, not systems/data:

python scripts/emit_primitives.py \
    <aisimulate>/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems "$BLIS_CATALOG"

and its output is a reference to compare the descriptor entries against, not a file to commit whole (see the warning at the end of this section). Two descriptor keys are deliberately not emitted — mem_empirical_constant_latency and p2p_latency — because nothing in BLIS reads them and a reader would double-count the measured floors (methodology §1). a100_pcie is skipped and the a100_sxm descriptor is scoped to both A100 names (methodology §5).

The GEMM envelope re-derives, and is checked against the committed value, with its owner:

python scripts/relane_gemm_envelope.py --check

docs.title: cost-model-collectives.yaml — generated
docs.text:
This set is generated in two passes, because its entries come from two different lanes.

python scripts/emit_collectives.py "$AISIMULATE_DATA" > /tmp/collectives-nccl.yaml

That regenerates the NCCL-sourced entries. Checked against the committed file, all 435 entries that cite an NCCL collection reproduce with no value difference. The generator is pinned to the collections those entries cite (PINNED_NCCL: 2.27.3 for A100 and L40S, 2.29.2 elsewhere) rather than taking the newest directory. That pin matters: AISimulate has since added NCCL 2.30.7, which carries 60 rows under a narrower schema with no device or version column where 2.29.2 carries 504 under the full one, so "newest wins" would both crash and silently re-cite the entries. Set NCCL_COLLECTION to move a fit deliberately.

The remaining 45 entries are all all_reduce, and they do not come from NCCL. vLLM uses its own one-shot/two-shot kernel for any tensor-parallel all-reduce that fits the custom kernel's size limit, which AISimulate measures separately; on matched (num_gpus, message_size) pairs the custom kernel under CUDA graph is the faster by a median factor of 0.635, so an NCCL-derived coefficient over-charges a graph-mode all-reduce by about 1.6×. Those 45 ship from the vLLM lane:

python scripts/fit_collectives_vllm.py --all "$AISIMULATE_DATA"

Re-running the NCCL pass alone will therefore differ from the committed file on exactly those 45 entries, and on nothing else. A reproducer should expect that.

Every entry is method: measured. The 208 with fitted: true are curve fits; the remainder are order statistics — a floor is the minimum over the size-independent region, not a regression — which is why they are fitted: false while still being measurements with their own Parquet citation.

The 72 _a100_80 entries are the one group the NCCL pass cannot emit from this checkout: a100_pcie ships no comm/ tree. They are scoped to a100-80 and carry the A100-SXM measurement — 63 citing a100_sxm/comm/nccl/2.27.3, the other 9 the vLLM custom-all-reduce sweep — so each names the sweep it actually comes from rather than claiming an A100-PCIe measurement that does not exist. Treating the two A100 80GB parts as one for collectives is a modelling choice, recorded in each entry's rationale.

docs.title: cost-model-attention.yaml — fitted per part
docs.text:
Decode (attention_decode_floor, attention_decode_rate), fitted on the vLLM lane:

python scripts/fit_attention.py "$AISIMULATE_DATA"/h200_sxm/attention/vllm/0.25.0 --chip h200

which prints attention_decode_floor 13.5 us and 0.54 of 4.800 TB/s — that is the committed attention_decode_rate of 2,592,000 bytes/µs — over 34,818 full-attention points, the count its citation records.

Prefill (attention_prefill_floor, attention_prefill_work_scale):

# Five parts have a vLLM 0.25.0 context-attention sweep.
python scripts/fit_attention_prefill.py --collection vllm/0.25.0 \
    h200_sxm:h200 h100_sxm:h100 b200_sxm:b200 b300_sxm:b300 gb200:gb200-nvl72

# L40S and A100 do not. Each ships from the newest vLLM lane that has one,
# which is what their `sources` entries cite.
python scripts/fit_attention_prefill.py --collection vllm/0.24.0 l40s:l40s
python scripts/fit_attention_prefill.py --collection vllm/0.14.0 a100_sxm:a100-sxm

Expected output, matching the committed entries and the point counts in their citations:

part lane floor µs work_scale points h200 vllm/0.25.0 18.5 0.44 27,693 h100 vllm/0.25.0 19.5 0.44 27,693 b200 vllm/0.25.0 16.5 0.38 27,574 b300 vllm/0.25.0 15.0 0.44 27,574 gb200-nvl72 vllm/0.25.0 17.0 0.38 27,574 l40s vllm/0.24.0 13.0 0.50 26,267 a100-sxm vllm/0.14.0 19.5 0.50 5,457

--collection defaults to trtllm/1.3.0rc20, the lane an earlier revision of these coefficients was fitted on, so that fit also stays reproducible; pass the lane explicitly for the values currently committed. Only full attention is fitted — rows with a non-zero window_size read a bounded number of bytes, and fitting them together would fit one curve to two byte counts.

docs.title: cost-model-recurrent.yaml — fitted per family
docs.text:
# KDA (Kimi-K3), h100 / h200 / gb300. Re-derives all six entries and diffs them
# against the committed file; --insert CHIP adds a part the set does not carry yet.
python scripts/relane_recurrent_kda.py --check

# MAMBA2 (Nemotron-3-Ultra). The model filter is required to reproduce the committed
# values: this sweep carries six geometries and pooling them fits none of them.
python scripts/fit_recurrent.py \
    "$AISIMULATE_DATA"/h100_sxm/linear_attention/trtllm/1.3.0rc20/mamba2_perf.parquet \
    --model nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-NVFP4

The second prints n=11 floor=3.5us rate=8.50 tok/us geo-err 1.120x, which is both committed *_mamba2 value and the error its rationale states. Without --model the same command pools 66 rows across six models and prints 4.2/23.25 — a number that is in the file's history nowhere and should not be mistaken for a refit.

The KDA command prints h100 3.8us/0.235, h200 4.3us/0.237 and gb300 7.4us/0.457, which are the committed values. Do not fit KDA from kda/sglang/0.5.16 or take the kda_fused_decode row: an earlier revision of this guide did, and both are wrong. fused_kda_decode is AMD-only — vllm/models/kimi_k3/amd/ops/kda_decode.py gates on gfx942/gfx950 — so it runs on no CUDA deployment, and vLLM's NVIDIA path (nvidia/kda.py:980-993) runs causal_conv1d_update then fused_recurrent_kda_packed_decode, so a layer costs the sum. The superseded recipe gives floor 5.1 µs and rate 1.50 tok/µs, a rate 6.4× too fast.

What this data does and does not cover matters more here than anywhere else in the registry, and the script's header says it: KDA (Kimi-K3) is complete, carrying the convolution and the recurrent scan separately plus a fused decode variant. MAMBA2 is not — the sweep has only causal_conv1d_fn and causal_conv1d_update, so the committed *_mamba2 pair is the convolution alone and is a documented LOWER BOUND on a Mamba2 layer, not its cost. The selective-scan kernel is in no collection in the tree.

docs.title: Sliding-window attention — *_swa
docs.text:
The windowed entries are fitted by a separate script, because a windowed kernel reads a number of bytes bounded by the window rather than by the context. scripts/relane_attention_swa.py owns them and reads its values from scripts/fit_attention_by_kind.py:

python scripts/relane_attention_swa.py --collection vllm/0.25.0 --check

The windowed entries were relaned from TRT-LLM to vLLM (methodology §7.1), and each entry's citation names the collection it was fitted on: vllm/0.25.0 on the Hopper and Blackwell parts, vllm/0.24.0 on L40S, whose newest vLLM collection that is. Pass the collection the entry cites; the A100 pair is assumed and is written by extrapolate_by_generation.py instead.

Using the context length for both kinds is what made an early windowed fit land at 2.00 of datasheet peak — a physically impossible rate, and the reason the two kinds are fitted apart rather than together.

docs.title: InferenceX CollectiveX run bodies ($COLLECTIVEX_DATA)
docs.text:
Three writers read CollectiveX run bodies: fit_deepep_ll_graph.py, fit_host_link.py and fit_deepep_collectivex.py. Fetch the run list and each body from

https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/api/v1/collectivex/runs?version=1
https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/api/v1/collectivex/runs/<run_id>?version=1

and save each body as cx_run_<run_id>.body. The query must be the bare integer version=1: without it, or with v1, the API answers {"error":"Unknown version"}. The API keeps only its latest 15 runs, so a cited run can stop being fetchable. Each writer checks that the bodies its committed entries cite are present and hash to the cited sha256. If they are not, it exits 3 rather than re-fit and re-cite the entries on other runs, and validator/test_deepep_ll_graph.py skips with "the cited CollectiveX bodies are not present". The entries fit_deepep_ll_graph.py and fit_host_link.py wrote cite runs the API no longer serves (33356406487, 36334392363, 36367074689, 36402856875, and the swap_blocks bodies sha256 26cad6ccbdaa). They stay as committed, and those two gates skip until the bodies are restored.

docs.title: cost-model-host-overheads.yaml — not derived from either dataset
docs.text: All seven entries are method: assumed and none is fitted. These are host-side costs that neither dataset isolates — the script header notes that several could move to measured without cluster time, and should. Three of them cite the removed trained-physics set as an order-of-magnitude anchor only — the values there were fitted against a different functional form, and a coefficient is valid only for the form it was fitted against. The citations name the git SHA where that file can still be read.

docs.title: cost-model-memory.yaml — AISimulate's memory model, and vLLM's own logs
docs.text:
scripts/emit_memory.py writes the whole file, and --check gates it.

  • The activation multiples and floor are vendor_spec, read with ast from AISimulate's aisimulate_core/sdk/backends/ (located from $AISIMULATE_DATA, two directories up). Verified against AISimulate 70305030.
  • The CUDA-graph capture bytes are assumed, the median per mode of the committed docs/vllm-cudagraph-capture-samples.csv. That CSV is regenerated from the vLLM issue tracker, which needs an authenticated gh and changes as issues are filed — so a re-mine is a deliberate data update, committed with its diff, not part of --check:
python scripts/mine_vllm_cudagraph_memory.py fetch   /tmp/vllm-cg-cache
python scripts/mine_vllm_cudagraph_memory.py extract /tmp/vllm-cg-cache \
    > docs/vllm-cudagraph-capture-samples.csv
python scripts/emit_memory.py            # then review the value diff

The capture half needs no AISimulate tree, so test_capture_bytes_re_derive_from_the_committed_samples runs it in CI. Methodology §11 gives the composition these terms enter and why each is scoped as it is.

docs.title: Every committed value, and the one command that regenerates it
docs.text:
The table below is the reproducibility contract: each family names the script that owns it, and each of those scripts takes --check, which re-runs its own fitter and exits non-zero if the committed file would change. validator/test_writers_are_idempotent.py runs them all, and test_every_fitted_family_has_a_writer fails if a fitted family appears with no owner — so a value that cannot be regenerated cannot be added.

docs.title: Adding a part — the GB300 worked example
docs.text:
Every fitted family has a writer with --check (it re-runs its own fitter and exits non-zero if the committed file would change) and --insert CHIP (it appends a part the set does not carry yet, through the same renderer, so an inserted entry is byte-identical to what a later re-run produces). The order matters in one place: prefill attention reads the bf16 GEMM ramp from the registry, so the envelope must be committed first.

export AISIMULATE_DATA=<aisimulate>/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data
export BLIS_CATALOG=<path-to-blis-catalog>

# 1. descriptors (vendor_spec, from NVIDIA's own systems/gb300.yaml)
#    emit_primitives.py owns this family; its GEMM/MoE path is superseded — see below.
# 2. GEMM ramp, then MoE imbalance
python scripts/relane_gemm_envelope.py  --insert gb300
python scripts/relane_moe_imbalance.py  --insert gb300
# 3. attention: decode, then prefill (needs the ramp from step 2), then windowed
python scripts/relane_attention_decode.py  --insert gb300 gb300:gb300
python scripts/relane_attention_prefill.py --insert gb300 gb300:gb300
python scripts/relane_attention_swa.py     --insert gb300 gb300:gb300
# 4. recurrent
python scripts/relane_recurrent_kda.py     --insert gb300 gb300:gb300
# 5. collectives, per operator from the lane each belongs on
python scripts/insert_collectives_part.py --chip gb300 --sku gb300

Then assert idempotence, which is what makes the result auditable:

for s in relane_gemm_envelope relane_moe_imbalance relane_attention_decode \
         relane_attention_prefill relane_attention_swa relane_recurrent_kda; do
    python scripts/$s.py --check || echo "$s DRIFTED"
done
python -m pytest validator/ -q

Do not run emit_primitives.py or emit_collectives.py to regenerate a whole set. Both predate lane decisions that moved families off them. emit_primitives.py's COLLECTIONS table still pins trtllm/1.3.0rc20 while every committed gemm_* entry cites a vLLM lane (5be809b), and regenerating cost-model-collectives.yaml from NCCL gives 144 removals and 36 changes — all 36 being the all_reduce entries 2f71dd6 moved to vLLM's custom kernel, so it would silently re-introduce a 3.4× mispricing. Use the per-family writers; they are what --check guards.

docs.title: 4. Why the registry holds only what the kernel reads
docs.text:
blis-latency-kernel requests five sets — cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives, cost-model-host-overheads, cost-model-attention, cost-model-recurrent — and when the removals below were made coefficients/ held exactly those, 724 entries.

A sixth, cost-model-memory, is the one deliberate exception, and it is committed ahead of its reader rather than without one: it supplies magnitudes the kernel was hardcoding (inference-sim/blis-registry#33), and the kernel change that reads them, inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel#22, is sequenced to land after it. Until then no scenario lists it. The rule this section states still applies: if that reader does not land, the set should go.

Four sets were removed because nothing in BLIS read them; they are recoverable from git history, where they last appear at 8d78ff8:

set what it held why it went communication-coefficients.yaml 10 named TP/MoE collectives the kernel prices collectives from cost-model-collectives; 9 of its 10 entries were assumed/copied placeholders, 7 of them the value 1.0 pd-transfer-estimates.yaml PD KV-transfer base latency, fabric overhead PDTransferTime prices from catalog facts instead legacy-kv-transfer.yaml pre-#1590 CPU↔GPU transfer defaults TierTime prices from catalog facts instead lora-adapter-costs.yaml Digital-Twin adapter terms no consumer

The kernel's TierTime and PDTransferTime take their numbers from blis-catalog hardware facts — StorageDevice read/write bandwidths and base latency, IntraNodeBwGBps, InterNodeBwGBps — using only host_link_bandwidth from cost-model-primitives as a host-link ceiling. inference-sim does not read any of the four either; its own defaults.yaml carries the values its backends use.

The removal was verified to change nothing measurable. Scored against the InferenceX measured tier (-config-tier measured -framework vllm -length-range-ratio 1.0), the before and after reports are identical after stripping timestamps — every summary table, every GPU family, every model, the same n:

registry TPOT shape TPOT mape TTFT shape TTFT mape 747 entries, 9 sets 11.60% 13.52% 15.32% 50.68% 724 entries, 5 sets 11.60% 13.52% 15.32% 50.68%

Both runs used one binary, one catalog revision and one kernel revision, varying only the registry — the figures move with the catalog, so a comparison across catalog revisions proves nothing. n is 292/360/288/356.

Anyone extending the kernel to price offload tiers, PD transfer or LoRA should expect to calibrate those terms rather than recover them from history: the removed values were placeholders and transcriptions, not measurements.

docs.title: 5. Checking a re-derivation
docs.text:
python -m pytest validator/ -q        # derivation / value-preservation gates (schema validation lives in blis-schemas)
python scripts/validate_against_aisimulate_tables.py   # oracle check against AISimulate's own tables

A re-fit that lands on a different number is not automatically a correction. This registry has recorded six independently verified per-primitive improvements that each made end-to-end accuracy worse, because the composed model's accuracy rests on partially cancelling errors. No per-primitive refit ships on the strength of its own fit quality alone; see the standing rule in methodology.md.

docs.title: 6. Reproducing the evaluation figures exactly
docs.text: The accuracy numbers quoted for this registry are reproducible, but three details decide whether a reader gets the same figures, and each has silently produced wrong numbers during this work.

docs.title: 6.1 The scorer is not on main
docs.text:
Status (2026-10-30). inference-sim#1851 merged on 2026-10-13 (0d092d4), and the kernel-exclusive branch below no longer exists. The scorer now lives at tools/metricscore on inference-sim/inference-sim main. scripts/compare_registries.py still runs go run ./cmd/metricscore from /private/tmp/blis-kernel-wt, so it needs that path updated before it can run. The scorer also needs three corpora (-corpus aisimulate_e2e.json, -engine-settings inferencex_engine_settings.json, -absolutes inferencex_absolutes.json, or BLIS_MEASUREMENTS). blis-latency-kernel does not distribute them: its testdata/README.md says they are extracted from third-party publications by scripts/extract_*. Only aisimulate_e2e.json was available for the Muse Spark change (#60), so that change ships without an end-to-end score; see the change's pull request. Separately, no committed scenario lists cost-model-collectives-inferencex or cost-model-fabric (the scenarios list six sets, cost-model-primitives to cost-model-memory). An end-to-end score of entries in those two sets is therefore unchanged by construction until a scenario names them.

cmd/metricscore exists only on the kernel-exclusive branch of the sriumcp/inference-sim fork, the head of the still-open inference-sim#1851. inference-sim/inference-sim carries neither that branch nor the command, and a checkout of its main fails with stat cmd/metricscore: directory not found.

git clone --branch kernel-exclusive https://github.com/sriumcp/inference-sim /tmp/blis-scorer
cd /tmp/blis-scorer

docs.title: 6.2 -registry defaults to the sibling checkout, not to your work
docs.text:
The flag's default is /Users/sri/Documents/Projects/blis-registry — the main checkout. Scoring a branch or worktree without passing -registry explicitly scores the other registry and reports figures that do not belong to the tree under test. Always pass it:

go run ./cmd/metricscore \
  -config-tier measured -framework vllm -length-range-ratio 1.0 \
  -registry /path/to/the/registry/under/test

docs.title: 6.3 The three flags each change every figure
docs.text:
flag omitted passed -config-tier measured mixes measured and resolved configurations in one average only the 68 sweeps whose engine settings come from the run's own command line -framework vllm scores every framework, which only the published arms can do the subset BLIS models -length-range-ratio 1.0 AISimulate's one-sided [0.8·len, len] sampling constant prompt lengths, which is what vLLM's client produces with no --random-range-ratio

On the main-checkout kernel (a9b60e1) and registry (ea08479), the same command with and without -length-range-ratio 1.0 gives 11.62/12.05/15.23/52.94 and 11.22/12.19/16.22/57.13 respectively. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions, and a figure quoted without its flags cannot be checked.

docs.title: 6.4 Which tier to weigh
docs.text: inferencex_engine_settings.json records 68 sweeps with a captured engine-args log and 136 without, each of the latter listed in its incomplete array with reason: "no engine-args log". For the 136 the engine configuration is inferred from vLLM's defaults rather than observed, so an error on those points is as likely to be a wrong assumed configuration as a wrong model. The measured tier is the only one where the simulated deployment is ground truth, and it is the tier on which a coefficient change can be attributed to the model.

docs.title: 6.5 Rebuild the kernel between runs
docs.text: go run recompiles, but a pre-built binary does not. A stale binary has invalidated a result during this work. When scoring repeatedly, build once per kernel revision and name the binary after it.

docs.title: The registry in BLIS
docs.text:
A latency estimate depends on three kinds of number, and BLIS keeps them apart:

Declared facts What a vendor states about a model or a chip: layer counts, head dimensions, peak FLOP rates, memory bandwidth. Someone wrote them down; nothing about them is learned. They live in blis-catalog. Learned numbers What a cost model needs but no datasheet states: the latency floor of a decode attention kernel on an H200, the bandwidth an 8-rank all-reduce actually reaches, the token count at which a GEMM gets halfway to peak efficiency. They are obtained by fitting measurements, or assumed where no measurement exists. They live here. Deployment choices What a particular run selects: the GPU, the parallelism, the engine settings. They are stated per run, in a scenario, and committed nowhere.

The test for which side of the first line a number falls on is simple: could a measurement revise it? A chip's SM count cannot be revised by a benchmark; its achievable bandwidth can. The first belongs in the catalog, the second in the registry.

docs.title: Five repositories
docs.text:
Repository Holds Relationship to the registry blis-schemas Go types and validators; no data Defines what a coefficient set may contain and rejects any file that breaks the rules. The registry's CI runs its validator on every pull request. blis-catalog Models, chips, fabrics, workloads: declared facts The registry's scope.hardware values are the catalog's chip names (h200, gb200-nvl72, …). blis-registry Coefficient sets: learned numbers with provenance — blis-latency-kernel The cost model: prices one forward pass Reads coefficient sets by name and evaluates its cost laws with them. Holds no numbers of its own. inference-sim The discrete-event simulator (BLIS) Calls the kernel once per simulated step. The kernel-backed path is inference-sim#1851, branch kernel-exclusive of the sriumcp/inference-sim fork.

Dependencies run one way. blis-schemas depends on no other BLIS repository. The catalog and the registry are data, validated against the schemas. The kernel imports the schemas and reads the catalog and registry from disk at run time. The simulator imports the kernel. Nothing imports the simulator.

docs.title: What happens at run time
docs.text:
A scenario names everything a run needs, including which coefficient sets to use:

kind: Scenario
name: kimi-k3-h100-nospec
engine_version: "0.29.0"
model: kimi-k3
coefficients: [cost-model-primitives, cost-model-collectives, cost-model-host-overheads, cost-model-attention, cost-model-recurrent]
cluster:
  hardware: h100
  ...

(Abridged from testdata/kimi-k3-h100-nospec.yaml in blis-latency-kernel.)

The kernel then does three things with the registry, once, before the first step:

  1. Loads each named set from <registry>/coefficients/<name>.yaml with blis-schemas' strict loader, then validates it with the same schema rules the registry's CI runs. A file that fails either is refused before anything is priced.
  2. Filters by scope. An entry applies only if its scope admits the deployment: an entry scoped to hardware: [h200] is skipped on an H100. A dimension the scope does not mention is unconstrained.
  3. Resolves names. Sets apply in the order the scenario lists them; if two admitted entries share a name, the later one wins.

The result is a fixed table of numbers the kernel's cost laws read for the rest of the run.

What happens when a name is absent is the kernel's decision, made term by term in its new.go. Some lookups are required and fail with an error naming the missing coefficient. Many others fall back, usually to zero, so a part with no entry for a family has that term priced at nothing, and the run still completes. This is why coverage matters: the recurrent set fits every part its sweeps measure for exactly this reason.

docs.title: Why the learned numbers have their own repository
docs.text:
Because a learned number is only as good as the evidence behind it, and the evidence has to travel with the number. Putting coefficients in a repository of their own means each one can carry its method, its sources and its scope; can be re-derived and checked in CI independently of the code that uses it; and can be changed by a pull request whose diff shows exactly which numbers moved. A change here alters every estimate that uses the affected sets the next time the files are read; no code is rebuilt.

Next: what a coefficient records.

docs.title: A constant in a law
docs.text:
The kernel prices each primitive with a closed-form law. The registry supplies the constants in those laws, and nothing else. Three examples:

Primitive Law the kernel evaluates Constants the registry supplies Dense GEMM efficiency(M) = εmax · M / (M + M½) gemm_eps_max_<dtype>, gemm_m_half_<dtype> Decode attention latency = floor + KV bytes / rate attention_decode_floor, attention_decode_rate Collective latency = max(floor + size / rt, size / rpeak) collective_floor_…, collective_transition_rate_…, collective_peak_rate_…

The division matters. A law is code, reviewed as code, and the same for every part. A constant is data, specific to a part, and carries the evidence for its value. A constant is never a correction for one model: if a model is mispriced, the remedy is in the law or in the evidence, not in a per-model fudge factor.

It also means a coefficient is only meaningful for the law it was fitted against. Two constants with similar names in models of different form are different quantities. This is why sets do not inherit from one another.

docs.title: What an entry records
docs.text:
Each coefficient is one entry, keyed by its name:

Field Required Records value yes The number. Finite. units yes Its dimension, from a closed list (us_per_transfer, bytes_per_us, tokens, …). method yes How the value was obtained. See below. fitted yes Whether a curve fit produced it. scope yes Where it applies. See below. sources by method Citations: the exact file a value came from, and its role. rationale by method Why this value: what it replaced, what would replace it, where it is weak. ci95 no An interval [low, high] that must contain the value.

The file format lists every field and rule exactly.

docs.title: Method: how the value was obtained
docs.text:
The method is the field that keeps a measurement distinguishable from a guess. It is never inferred; the author states it.

measured Obtained from a measurement this project can re-run. Cites the data it came from. vendor_spec Taken from a vendor's own figure: here, the values NVIDIA ships in AISimulate's system descriptors and its memory model. NVIDIA observed or tuned them; this project did not. Requires a source. assumed An estimate arrived at by reasoning, where no dataset this project reads measures the quantity. Requires a rationale; by this registry's convention it also names the measurement that would replace the value. A careful estimate is still assumed. not_charged A deliberate zero, so that "this costs nothing" is distinguishable from "this cost is unknown". A value of zero under any other method is rejected.

The schema also defines literature (a published result not reproduced here), copied (carried over from another scope, which copied_from names) and, since blis-schemas v0.4.0, calibrated (back-solved through the cost model from end-to-end measured cases, which it cites as measured_case sources, with the held-out metrics in validated). No committed entry uses any of the three.

fitted is separate from method because the two answer different questions. A vendor_spec value is never fitted. A measured value may be fitted (the GEMM ramp) or not (an order statistic of measured ratios, like the MoE routing imbalance). The schema allows fitted: true only with method: measured or calibrated.

docs.title: Scope: where the value holds
docs.text:
A scope lists the deployments an entry applies to, along five dimensions: hardware, model, tp, ep and nodes_spanned. Every committed entry is scoped by hardware alone, using the catalog's chip names.

Three rules govern it:

  • A stated dimension restricts; an unstated one does not. An entry scoped to hardware: [h200] applies to every model and parallelism on an H200, and to nothing else.
  • An empty scope is an error, not a wildcard. A coefficient whose applicability is not stated cannot be applied safely, so the schema refuses it.
  • An entry's identity is its name and its scope. One set may hold gemm_eps_max_bf16 for h100 and again for h200; the kernel picks by scope. Two entries with the same name and the same scope are rejected, because only one could be used.

Some quantities vary along dimensions that are not scope keys, such as data type, collective operation and rank count. Those ride in the name: collective_floor_all_reduce_fp16_8rank_h200. The collective names also carry the part, because the kernel constructs those keys from the chip name.

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
A coefficient set is one YAML file under coefficients/, naming itself (name: cost-model-attention) and listing its entries. Sets are standalone: no file extends another, and a scenario that wants several lists them all. If two listed sets hold the same name for the same part, the one listed later is used.

How entries are grouped into sets follows the evidence as much as the primitive. The seven host overheads are all assumed and are kept in their own set so that no reader takes the provenance of a mostly measured set to be uniform. The memory-occupancy magnitudes are kept apart from the primitives because they rest on a different source.

Most sets are written by a script, not by hand. Their headers say so, and the committed file is whatever the script prints; Contributing a change explains why that matters.

Next: where the numbers come from.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
The registry draws on public data only, and gives each dataset one job. Keeping the jobs separate is what lets an accuracy figure mean something: a dataset used to fit a number cannot also be the evidence that the number is right.

Dataset What it measures Its job here NVIDIA AISimulate operator sweeps One kernel at a time (a GEMM, an attention call, a collective) across many shapes, per GPU and per serving engine Fitting. Every measured entry comes from these sweeps. AISimulate system descriptors and memory model NVIDIA's own per-part corrections and capacity figures Transcription. The source of every vendor_spec entry. AISimulate FPM One whole forward pass at a known batch and KV composition Validation and model selection. It may fit only a term that is itself about the whole pass. SemiAnalysis InferenceX End-to-end serving runs, with a scheduler and a client Evaluation only. Never used to fit or select anything. vLLM start-up logs in vLLM's issue tracker CUDA-graph capture memory on real deployments Anchoring the magnitude of four assumed memory entries.

docs.title: Why a sweep can fit a constant and a forward pass cannot
docs.text: An operator sweep varies one primitive with everything else held fixed, so it identifies that primitive's two or three constants and nothing else. A whole-forward measurement is one number per batch: the sum over every layer and every resource. Many assignments of constants produce the same sum, so fitting a per-primitive constant to it would attribute to that constant whatever every other term gets wrong. This is a fact about identifiability, not a policy, and it does not change as the dataset grows.

docs.title: Fit the engine you predict
docs.text:
AISimulate measures the same operator under several serving engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM) and collective libraries (NCCL). BLIS predicts vLLM. Where the engines run different kernels, the measurements differ, sometimes in sign between GPU generations, so an entry is fitted on the lane that matches what vLLM executes. Where vLLM delegates to NCCL, as it does for every collective except all-reduce, the NCCL lane is vLLM's path. Where the engines share kernels, the lanes agree and the choice is made on data volume.

The rule is applied per operator, and the decisions are recorded with their evidence in the methodology. The current state, computed from each entry's primary citation when this page was built:
