docs.title: A better fit can be a worse model
docs.text: The kernel's accuracy rests partly on errors that cancel. A correction that improves one primitive's fit can make the end-to-end estimate worse, because it removes an error that was offsetting another. This has happened six times in this project. So no per-primitive fit is committed without an end-to-end check, and a correction whose offsetting term has not been identified waits.

docs.title: Gaps are declared, not filled
docs.text: Where no dataset measures a quantity, the entry says so: it is assumed, its rationale states the reasoning, and it names the measurement that would replace it. The host overheads are the clearest case. No public dataset times an engine's Python path on the parts these entries price, so all seven are assumed, and each entry describes the experiment that would measure it. (FPM's GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM leaves on GB300 time the scheduler's per-request cost indirectly; they are held-out evidence, not a fit, see the methodology §10.7.)

docs.title: Every measured number can be re-derived
docs.text:
Each generated set is written by a script that its header names, and the scripts are pure functions of their input data: given the same AISimulate collection, they print the same file. The registry's derivation tests re-run them and compare the output with what is committed, so a value edited by hand, or a citation that no longer reproduces its value, fails.

Those tests need a local clone of AISimulate. CI does not fetch one, so on a pull request they skip and say why; the schema gate and the property tests run on every pull request regardless. Validation lists what runs where, and Reproducing the coefficients is the step-by-step guide.

For the full argument behind each rule, with the measurements and the retractions, read the methodology.

docs.title: Contributing a change
docs.text: Most changes to the registry change numbers that every estimate using the affected sets will read. The process below exists so that each such change is visible, reproducible and checked at the level the numbers are used at.

docs.title: Rules that apply to every change
docs.text:
Never edit a generated value by hand. Most sets are written by a script, and the header of each file says which. Change the script or its input, re-run it, and commit what it prints. A hand edit is indistinguishable from a typo, and the derivation tests will reject it when they run against the data.

A value and its citation move together. An entry's sources must name the exact collection the value was fitted on. Changing one without the other is how a registry comes to describe a fit nobody ran.

One collection per part, per family. Fit on a single engine release. Mixing collections changes the row set silently and makes a difference between two parts reflect software rather than silicon.

Fitting data never includes evaluation data. A fitter must not read InferenceX or SemiAnalysis results; scripts/select_overlap_band.py holds the guard to import.

No per-primitive fit ships without an end-to-end check. A better fit to one primitive has, six times in this project, made the overall estimate worse. Score the change with scripts/compare_registries.py (see methodology §6.1) and report the before and after figures in the pull request.

A coefficient with no reader is not live. Before adding a family, confirm that blis-latency-kernel looks the key up. Search the kernel for the name, not the registry.

docs.title: The usual workflow
docs.text:
1. Set up the data. Clone AISimulate and a blis-catalog checkout, and export their paths:

    git clone https://github.com/ai-dynamo/aisimulate
export AISIMULATE_DATA=$PWD/aisimulate/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data
export BLIS_CATALOG=/path/to/blis-catalog
pip install -r requirements-fit.txt

    requirements.txt covers the property tests. requirements-fit.txt adds what the fitters need to read the Parquet sweeps: pyarrow, pandas and numpy.

  2. Run the family's writer. The writer table names the script that owns each family. Each takes --check, which exits non-zero if the committed file would change, and most take --insert CHIP to add a part.

  3. Run the derivation tests with the data present. CI does not run them on pull requests (the rederive workflow takes ~20 minutes and is manual-dispatch only), so run them locally before any pull request that touches a coefficient, a writer or a test. With COLLECTIVEX_DATA also set to the CollectiveX run bodies:

    scripts/rederive.sh

    It runs python -m pytest validator/ -q -rs and fails on any skip other than the by-design ramp-form ones, because a skip with the data present is a test that did not run.

  4. Run the schema validator. CI runs it on every pull request; running it first saves a round trip. From a blis-schemas checkout at the tag pinned in .github/workflows/validate.yml:

    go run ./cmd/validate-registry /path/to/blis-registry

  5. Score the change end to end, as above, if it changes a value a step time depends on.

  6. Preview the documentation. The reference pages are generated from coefficients/, so they show your change:

    pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve

  7. Open a pull request. Three checks run: schema-validate, derivation-tests and docs. All three must pass.

docs.title: Adding a part
docs.text:
A part must exist in blis-catalog before the registry can scope an entry to it, because scope.hardware uses catalog chip names. The order of the writers matters in one place (prefill attention reads the GEMM ramp from the registry), so follow the GB300 worked example.

The host-overhead and memory sets list every catalog part in their scope, and a property test checks that they do. Adding a part is therefore also a visible edit to those sets, which is intended: it is the reminder that their values were never measured on the new part.

docs.title: Adding a set
docs.text: Add the file under coefficients/, then add a reference page for it at docs/reference/sets/<name>.md and list that page in the nav of mkdocs.yml. The documentation build fails until both exist, so a set cannot be committed without a page. Copy an existing page; the table on it is generated, so the page needs only a short description of what the set prices and where its values come from.

docs.title: Writing documentation
docs.text: The pages under docs/ are Markdown, built with Material for MkDocs. A number that describes the registry's contents (a count, a value, a census) must not be typed into a page. Use a registry: directive instead, which the build computes from the committed files; docs_hooks/registry.py lists them. A retyped count is correct on the day it is written and wrong after the next refit.

docs.title: Changes across the repositories
docs.text: A change that also touches blis-schemas, the catalog, the kernel or inference-sim follows Changes across the repositories, which links the canonical process and lists the registry's own steps.

docs.title: Changes across the repositories
docs.text:
The process for a change that spans blis-schemas, blis-catalog, this registry, blis-latency-kernel and inference-sim is described once, in blis-schemas: [Changes across the repositories](https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-schemas/blob/main/docs/contributing/cross-repo-changes.md). This page lists only what is specific to the registry.

The registry depends on blis-schemas and on the catalog's part names; the kernel's tests and inference-sim read it. It is pushed after blis-schemas and before inference-sim.

docs.title: The standard for a coefficient or pricing change
docs.text: Every change to a coefficient, or to how a value is fitted, follows Fitting BLIS to the real world: a fit / held-out split declared before the held-out numbers are read, distributions rather than point errors, agreement across latency, KV, queueing and throughput, the version rule, and the landing gate. Contributing a change gives the workflow.

docs.title: When blis-schemas changes
docs.text: Move the blis-schemas ref in .github/workflows/validate.yml to the pushed head's full SHA, marked TEMPORARY with its pull request, or to the release tag before merge; see Moving the schema pin.

docs.title: When the catalog changes
docs.text: If the change needs a newer catalog, move CATALOG_SHA in .github/workflows/rederive.yml and the validator's vendored catalog files together, and run the derivation tests with the data present.

docs.title: When the registry changes
docs.text:
The kernel's tests pin the registry in testdata/upstream.lock, and inference-sim vendors it into testdata/registry with an .upstream-commit stamp. The vendored copy must equal this pull request's head, file for file, before any published number is computed from it.

A private-names check (.github/workflows/private-names.yml) reads its pattern from a repository secret and fails a pull request whose files, paths, commit messages, title or body match it.

docs.title: Cutting a release
docs.text:
1. Make sure main is green: schema-validate, derivation-tests and docs all pass.
  2. Run the derivation tests locally with the AISimulate data present (step 3 of the usual workflow). CI cannot run them.

  3. Publish the release from main:

    gh release create vX.Y.Z --target main --title vX.Y.Z --generate-notes

  4. Edit the notes to say which families changed, on which parts, and why, with links to the pull requests. A reader deciding whether to move to the release needs to know which estimates it affects.

docs.title: What publishing does
docs.text:
Publishing a release runs the docs workflow, which builds this site from the tag and publishes it as version X.Y.Z. If the tag is the highest release, latest moves to it; a patch to an older line is published under its own version and leaves latest alone. A pre-release (marked as such on GitHub, or tagged with a suffix such as -rc.1) is published under its own version and never becomes latest.

Every merge to main republishes dev (main). Every pull request builds the site with --strict and publishes nothing.

docs.title: Republishing a release's pages
docs.text:
To rebuild a release's documentation after fixing a page, run the workflow by hand:

gh workflow run docs.yml -f tag=vX.Y.Z

This builds the pages from main, so a fix lands without a new release, and generates the tables from the data. It first checks that coefficients/ on main is identical to the tag, and stops if it is not: the pages would describe numbers the release does not contain. Use the same command for a release that predates the documentation site.

docs.title: How the site is built
docs.text:
Material for MkDocs renders docs/, and mike keeps one copy per version on the gh-pages branch. The tables, counts and quoted entries are produced at build time by docs_hooks/registry.py, which reads coefficients/ and fails the build rather than render anything it cannot represent exactly. Its tests are in docs_hooks/test_registry.py.

To preview locally:

pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve

docs.title: Moving the schema pin
docs.text: The schema gate is pinned to a blis-schemas release in .github/workflows/validate.yml. A new blis-schemas release changes nothing here until the pin is moved, which is a one-line pull request whose CI run shows whether every committed set still loads. Update the tag named on File format in the same pull request.

A scenario names the sets it loads. The five cost-model-* sets for step time are the ones every committed scenario in blis-latency-kernel lists. Within them, a few families are committed but not looked up by the kernel. As of blis-latency-kernel e9cf217:

docs.title: Reading a set page
docs.text:
Each set page shows the set as a matrix: one row per coefficient, one column per part. A glyph before each value gives its method, and its shape alone identifies it:

Glyph Method ■ measured ◆ vendor_spec ○ assumed – not_charged

Every value is a link to its entry in the file, where the sources, rationale and scope are recorded. A dot (·) marks a part the set has no entry for. Whether that is an omission or a deliberate absence is stated in the set's header and on its page.

docs.title: Acceptance profiles
docs.text:
How far speculative decoding advances a request per verification step, by model, speculative method, K and thinking mode. Generated at build time from acceptance/, at revision [`v0.3.0`](https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry/tree/v0.3.0); nothing below is typed in by hand.

An acceptance-profile set is the acceptance counterpart of a coefficient set. Its format, and how a run resolves one value from it, are blis-schemas' acceptance reference (blis-schemas#65). Each profile holds the mean acceptance length (AL): the tokens a request gains per verification step, counting the target's bonus token, so it lies in [1, K + 1]. No per-position rates are stored. A consumer that needs them derives vLLM v0.31.0's minimum-variance schedule, which is how the InferenceX runs that force a published AL realise it.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
The set's own caveats, as committed:

  • Coding only. Every profile is SPEED-Bench's coding category, the only one InferenceX publishes; no other category has a value. A consumer must refuse other traffic, or fall back to coding with the substitution recorded; it must not substitute silently.
  • Measured on b300: deepseek-v4-pro, glm-5.2-fp8, glm-5.3, minimax-m3. Acceptance depends mostly on the model, drafter and workload rather than the chip; a resolution on another part records the reuse.
  • Measured on b200: deepseek-v4.1-flash. Acceptance depends mostly on the model, drafter and workload rather than the chip; a resolution on another part records the reuse.
  • deepseek-v4.1-flash dspark: the source file names no hardware. b200 is the part run 34493175056 ran on: its collect-al job 102924945774 ran on runner b200-nscale-slurm_00 (label cluster:b200-nscale) and launched runners/launch_b200-nscale-compat.sh with BENCH_BASE benchmarks/single_node/dsv41flash_fp4_b200.
  • deepseek-v4.1-flash with dspark at K 6-8 was rejected by the image vllm/vllm-openai:deepseekv41-flash-0909 (https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/34494319147), so those K have no value.
  • glm-5.3 mtp (K 3) is provisional: copied from glm5.2_mtp.yaml, not measured on glm-5.3.
  • Deployment precision. The fp4 in the collectors' names is the label speedbench-al.yml gives every collection (PRECISION fp4, and the _fp4_b300_vllm.sh name it requires), not the precision served. Each collector serves its model's checkpoint at that checkpoint's own weight precision, which is the catalog model's. At InferenceX 9fa76586ed1e: dsv4_fp4_b300_vllm.sh (deepseek-v4-pro) serves the staged checkpoint with no quantization flag, and --kv-cache-dtype fp8 (line 123); glm52_fp4_b300_vllm.sh (glm-5.2-fp8) serves the staged checkpoint with no quantization flag, and --kv-cache-dtype fp8 (line 131); minimaxm3_fp4_b300_vllm.sh (minimax-m3) serves the staged checkpoint, which its comment (lines 16-19) states is unquantized BF16, with no --kv-cache-dtype. kv_cache_dtype is recorded where a collector sets it; a collector may have changed since its run.
  • The source files for deepseek-v4-pro, glm-5.2-fp8, minimax-m3 name no engine image, so their engine_image reads "unrecorded: the source file names no engine image".
  • Not carried: dsv4-pro-0813-dspark.yaml (deepseek-v4-pro-0813), because its model deepseek-v4-pro-0813 is no catalog model's repository, and no alias maps it.
  • Not carried: kimik3_dspark.yaml (kimi-k3), because the two Kimi-K3 DSpark curves differ only in the draft sampler (greedy, and probabilistic with block rejection), which a profile's key cannot state, and InferenceX's own resolver (curves.py curve_name) refuses to pick one without it.
  • Not carried: kimik3_dspark_probabilistic_sample_method_block_rejection_sample_method.yaml (kimi-k3), because the two Kimi-K3 DSpark curves differ only in the draft sampler (greedy, and probabilistic with block rejection), which a profile's key cannot state, and InferenceX's own resolver (curves.py curve_name) refuses to pick one without it.
  • Not carried: minimaxm3_eagle3_gqa.yaml (minimax-m3), because it is the curve for the Inferact/MiniMax-M3-EAGLE3-GQA drafter and shares minimaxm3_eagle3's key, since a profile's key cannot state the drafter; InferenceX's resolver uses it only for a GQA drafter, and the base curve otherwise.
  • Not carried: qwen3.5_mtp.yaml (qwen3.5-397b-a17b-nvfp4), because its model qwen3.5-397b-a17b-nvfp4 is no catalog model's repository, and no alias maps it.
  • Not carried: qwen3.8next_mtp.yaml (qwen3.8-flash-next-fp8), because its model qwen3.8-flash-next-fp8 is no catalog model's repository, and no alias maps it.

docs.title: How the set is made
docs.text: scripts/emit_acceptance_profiles.py writes the file, and its --check is the drift gate, as for the coefficient writers. The rules it follows are in methodology §12.

docs.title: File format
docs.text: A coefficient set is a YAML file under coefficients/. The rules on this page are enforced by blis-schemas, at the release v0.4.0, in spec/coefficient and vocab, the release CI pins; it also validates acceptance/ and routing/. Where this page and the schema disagree, the schema is right.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
kind: CoefficientSet          # exactly this
name: cost-model-primitives   # the set's identity; scenarios refer to it by this name
coefficients:                 # a list; each item is a map with one key, the coefficient's name
  - <name>:
      <fields>

One entry from the committed sets, quoted from its file:

coefficients/cost-model-primitives.yaml, line 627
- gemm_eps_max_bf16:
    value: 1.0
    units: dimensionless
    method: measured
    fitted: true
    scope: {hardware: [h100]}
    sources:
      - {kind: model, cite: "NVIDIA AISimulate systems/data/h100_sxm/gemm/vllm/0.25.0/gemm_perf.parquet (NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3), 37,518 bfloat16 rows over 74 token counts, kernel torch.nn.functional.linear", role: primary}
    rationale: >
      The fraction of this part's bfloat16 peak a large, well-shaped matmul asymptotically reaches, on vLLM's own linear kernel rather than the generic `torch_flow` path the TRT-LLM sweep measures. Envelope rather than mean: a cost model predicts what a well-shaped GEMM achieves. Least-squares residual 0.0629 over 74 token counts.

Quoted from the committed file at build time.

Unknown keys are errors at every level: top level, entry, scope and source. A misspelled field is rejected, not ignored.

docs.title: Entry fields
docs.text:
Field Type Required Rule value number yes Finite. Zero only with method: not_charged. units term yes One of the units below. method term yes One of the methods below. fitted bool yes Must be present, even when false. true requires method: measured or calibrated. scope map yes At least one dimension. sources list by method If present, non-empty. Required for literature and vendor_spec; calibrated requires at least one of kind measured_case. rationale string by method Required for every method except measured. ci95 [low, high] no Finite, low ≤ high, and the value must lie inside. copied_from string for copied The scope the value was copied from. supersedes string no The entry this one replaces. validated metric or list for calibrated Metrics the value has been checked against. unsupported metric or list no Metrics it has explicitly not been checked against.

Within one set, no two entries may share both a name and a scope. Scope comparison ignores the order of values, so [h100, h200] and [h200, h100] are the same scope.

The registry's own tests add two requirements the schema leaves out: every measured entry cites a source, and every assumed entry carries a substantial rationale.

A source is {kind, cite, role}, all three required.

  • kind: discussion, publication, datasheet, model, vendor_doc, measured_case
  • role: primary, supporting, upper_bound
  • cite: free text, specific enough to find the exact file and rows

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
Names are snake_case. A name states the quantity, then the axes that vary it and are not scope keys, in a fixed order per family:

  • gemm_eps_max_<dtype>
  • attention_decode_floor_<kind>, with no suffix for full attention
  • collective_<param>_<op>_<dtype>_<N>rank_<chip>, where <chip> is the catalog name with - replaced by _
  • nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank, cudagraph_capture_bytes_<mode>

The kernel constructs these names when it looks a value up, so a name is an interface. Renaming one is a change to the kernel too.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Three kinds of check guard the registry. They answer different questions, and passing one says nothing about the others.

Check Question it answers Where it runs Schema Could a consumer load this file? CI, every pull request and every push to main Properties Is every value physically sensible, and is its provenance complete? CI, every pull request and every push to main Re-derivation Does every value still come out of its fitter, from its cited data? Locally, with an AISimulate clone; skipped in CI

The documentation build is a fourth, narrower check: it fails if a set has no reference page, or if a set holds data the reference tables cannot represent faithfully.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
The schema-validate job runs blis-schemas' own validator over every file under coefficients/:

go run ./cmd/validate-registry /path/to/blis-registry   # from a blis-schemas checkout

It applies exactly the rules a consumer applies when it loads a set: strict decoding, then field validation. The rules are listed on File format. The registry keeps no schema validator of its own, so there is one definition of a valid file, and it is the one the kernel uses.

blis-schemas is pinned to a release tag in .github/workflows/validate.yml. A schema release changes nothing here until the pin is moved.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
validator/test_coefficient_properties.py reads only the committed files and a vendored copy of the catalog's chip descriptors, so it always runs. Each test encodes a defect that this project has shipped at least once:

  • no bandwidth rate exceeds its part's datasheet peak, and every rate is a plausible fraction of it;
  • GEMM asymptotes are fractions; MoE imbalance is near one, and its 90th percentile is not below its median;
  • collective floors do not fall as the group widens, rates do not rise steeply, and no transition rate exceeds its peak rate;
  • recurrent floors are positive and bounded, and rates are slower than the convolution alone;
  • a kind-specific attention floor is not a module measurement in disguise;
  • the hardware-independent sets cover every catalog part;
  • every measured entry cites a source, and every assumed entry explains itself;
  • the memory set has a capture entry for every vLLM CUDA-graph mode, respects the capture-pool overlay, and its activation multiples fall with width; and the capture sizes re-derive from the committed log samples.

docs.title: Re-derivation
docs.text:
validator/test_generated_from_aisimulate.py and validator/test_writers_are_idempotent.py re-run the fitters and compare with the committed files. They need the AISimulate sweeps, which are not vendored here, and they skip when the data is absent, saying so. CI has no copy, so in CI they always skip.

Run them before any pull request that changes a fitted value, and before a release:

export AISIMULATE_DATA=/path/to/aisimulate/python/aisimulate/src/aisimulate_core/systems/data
export BLIS_CATALOG=/path/to/blis-catalog
export COLLECTIVEX_DATA=/path/to/collectivex-run-bodies
scripts/rederive.sh

scripts/rederive.sh is also what the manual-dispatch rederive workflow runs.

They check that:

  • each writer reproduces its committed file byte for byte (--check), and every fitted family has a writer;
  • the generated GEMM and collective values survive an independent re-derivation by a second code path;
  • the all-reduce entries come from the vLLM CUDA-graph lane specifically, since the eager lane is slower than NCCL and accepting it would misprice all-reduce by 3.4×;
  • in the primitive and collective sets, every source is NVIDIA's, and no assumed entry carries a foreign measurement in through its rationale.

A test that cannot run says why. Treat an unexpected skip as a test that did not run.

docs.title: The end-to-end check
docs.text: None of the above can tell whether a change makes BLIS more accurate. That needs the evaluation corpus and the scorer on the kernel-exclusive branch of the sriumcp/inference-sim fork (inference-sim#1851), and is described in methodology §6.1. evaluation-baseline.json records the last recorded figures, with the scorer and catalog revisions they were scored at.

docs.title: cost-model-attention
docs.text:
The constants for attention, by phase and by kind.

Decode is priced as a fixed setup cost plus a read of the KV cache:

latency = attention_decode_floor + KV bytes / attention_decode_rate

The floor is why a pure-bandwidth model is wrong at short context: an attention kernel costs on the order of 10 µs whatever the context. The rate is the bandwidth the kernel actually reaches, which on these parts is well short of the datasheet figure and varies too much between parts for one derate to serve.

Three kinds of attention carry their own pair, because each reads a different number of bytes:

Suffix Kind Read per step, per request none full attention (GQA) K and V for every cached token _swa sliding window K and V for at most the window's tokens _mla multi-head latent attention one compressed latent vector per cached token

The _mla floors are assumed: they are set from the part's own measured full-attention floor, because the tables they were first fitted on measured the whole MLA block, projections included, and the kernel prices those projections separately. Methodology §3 records how that was found. Sparse MLA has no pair of its own; §10 explains why none is fittable from this data.

Prefill is priced from the GEMM efficiency ramp, scaled by attention_prefill_work_scale, above a floor attention_prefill_floor. The scale is a fraction of the bf16 ramp in cost-model-primitives, so refitting that ramp means refitting this.

docs.title: cost-model-collectives-inferencex
docs.text:
DeepEP dispatch plus combine, priced as one MoE layer's all-to-all:

latency = floor + tokens · hidden · 2 · top_k / rate

with per-rank tokens. Two variants are here, both as InferenceX CollectiveX times them:

  • deepep_low_latency_graph: DeepEP's legacy low-latency kernels under CUDA-graph replay, which vLLM v0.31.0 uses for a captured decode step. The eager pair (moe_a2a_*_deepep_low_latency_<N>rank_<part> in cost-model-collectives) prices a step with no graph.
  • deepep_v2_graph: DeepEP v2's ElasticBuffer with vLLM deepep_v2's CUDA-graphs-on flags (no CPU sync, no expand). CollectiveX replays decode as a graph and runs prefill eager on the same path.

Where the values come from. InferenceX CollectiveX, backend deepep-v2, bf16, shape hidden 7168, top-6 of 384, uniform routing, the roundtrip p50 per tokens-per-rank point. The h100 and h200 8-rank pair (one node, NVLink) fits tokens 1/4/16/64/256 and holds out 2/8/32/128. GB200-NVL72 at 8 and 16 ranks (2 and 4 trays of one MNNVL rack) and H200 at 16 ranks (two nodes over 400G InfiniBand, scoped fabric: [ib-400g]) use the same split for the low-latency mode. The v2 mode adds the prefill ladder: it fits 1/4/16/64/256/1024/4096 and holds out 2/8/32/128/512/2048/8192. Each entry states its run, its body's sha256 and its held-out error. The H200 16-rank entries measure a virtualised pool's path, not the InfiniBand fabric, and say so.

Why a separate set. cost-model-collectives comes from a single source, NVIDIA AISimulate. A set that mixed the two methodologies would confound comparisons across parts. A scenario lists this set next to cost-model-collectives to take these prices. Without it, the kernel prices as before.

docs.title: cost-model-collectives
docs.text:
The constants for the four collectives the kernel prices: all-gather, all-reduce, all-to-all and reduce-scatter. Each configuration (operation, dtype, rank count, part) has three:

latency = max(floor + size / transition_rate, size / peak_rate)

The floor is the latency of a small message, where size no longer matters. The peak rate is the bandwidth a large message reaches. The transition rate governs the region in between, roughly 64 KiB to 8 MiB, where a two-parameter model is optimistic and where a prefill batch's collectives fall.

Operation, dtype and rank count are not scope keys, so they are part of the name, and so is the part, because the kernel builds the key from the chip name: collective_floor_all_reduce_fp16_8rank_h200. The tables below fold the part into the columns.

Where the values come from. All-reduce at fp16 is measured on vLLM's own custom all-reduce kernel on most parts; the other operations, and the int8 all-reduce, are measured on NCCL, which is what vLLM runs for them. The source table on Where the numbers come from gives the current split. Rank widths a part was never swept at are assumed, extrapolated from that part's own measured widths with a holdout-validated linear model, and each such entry states its predictor and holdout error. Methodology §8.5 gives the argument, including the model that was tried first and refuted.

The set also holds the MoE all-to-all that DeepEP dispatch plus combine costs, as floor + bytes / rate per backend, rank count and part (moe_a2a_floor_deepep_low_latency_8rank_h100). All of them come from AISimulate. The low-latency pair measured by CollectiveX under CUDA-graph replay is in cost-model-collectives-inferencex.

docs.title: cost-model-fabric
docs.text:
The effective / nominal bandwidth of each inter-node fabric class blis-catalog defines under networks/. A fabric's catalog figure, InterNodeBwGBps, is its line rate divided by eight, per GPU, per direction. A transfer over it achieves less. blis-latency-kernel multiplies the nominal rate by fabric_bandwidth_efficiency wherever bytes leave a node: a P/D handoff, a pipeline-stage boundary, and the cross-node share of a collective. It refuses a value outside (0, 1].

Each entry is scoped by the fabric's catalog identity (scope: {fabric: [ib-400g]}), not by hardware. A rack-wide NVLink domain (gb200-nvl72) belongs to the chip, so it is not corrected here.

Where the values come from. None is a measurement this project made.

  • ib-400g is literature: published nccl-tests all_reduce results on H100 hosts with eight ConnectX-7 400G InfiniBand NICs each (NVIDIA/nccl-tests#309), as a fraction of the 400 GB/s ceiling an NVIDIA maintainer states there.
  • roce-200g and ethernet-100gbe are assumed. No public multi-node measurement of either was found. Each rationale states the range the value could lie in and the one public datum that bounds it.

docs.title: cost-model-host-overheads
docs.text:
CPU time spent by the engine around the GPU work: tokenizing a prompt, launching kernels or replaying a captured CUDA graph, detokenizing each output token, and tearing down a finished request.

Every entry is assumed. No public dataset measures an engine's host path: AISimulate times kernels, FPM times one synchronized forward pass, and InferenceX is used for evaluation only. The values rest on reasoning and, for three of them, on the order of magnitude of an earlier BLIS fit against a different functional form. Each entry's rationale states its reasoning and the measurement that would replace it.

The set is kept separate from the measured sets so that its provenance is not mistaken for theirs. Its scope lists every catalog part because the work is CPU-side and has no per-part value; listing them makes adding a part a visible edit here.

Assumed is not the same as unimportant. The largest single accuracy movement recorded in this project, measured-tier TTFT error from 52.94% to 31.47%, came from one of these seven (methodology §6.0).

docs.title: cost-model-memory
docs.text:
The per-rank memory a deployment holds besides weights and KV cache. These numbers set how many sequences fit, not how long a step takes.

The terms add, per rank:

weights + activation + nccl_communicator_bytes_<N>rank + engine_workspace_bytes + cudagraph_capture_bytes_<mode>

with

activation = max(activation_buffer_count_<family>_<N>rank · max_num_batched_tokens · h · 2, activation_scratch_floor_bytes)

where family is dense or moe, N is min(tp, 8), and h is the attention width. The communicator and workspace terms are in cost-model-primitives, because NVIDIA's descriptors state them per part.

Two provenances. The activation multiples and floor are vendor_spec: NVIDIA's own memory model, as AISimulate's vLLM backend uses it. The CUDA-graph capture sizes are assumed: their magnitude is the median of vLLM's own start-up logs, collected from vLLM's issue tracker into a committed CSV (vllm-cudagraph-capture-samples.csv). FULL and FULL_DECODE_ONLY have too few samples and are charged the FULL_AND_PIECEWISE figure as an upper bound. NONE is a declared zero.

The kernel does not read this set yet; see blis-latency-kernel#22. Methodology §11 gives the composition and each scoping decision.

docs.title: cost-model-primitives
docs.text:
The constants for dense and grouped matrix multiplies, plus the per-part memory and link figures from NVIDIA's own system descriptors.

GEMM efficiency ramp (measured). The kernel prices a GEMM at a fraction of the part's dense peak for the dtype, rising with the token count M:

efficiency(M) = gemm_eps_max_<dtype> · M / (M + gemm_m_half_<dtype>)

Both constants are fitted per part and per dtype on AISimulate's GEMM sweeps. They have to be per part: H100 and H200 share a die and their asymptotes agree, but their knees do not, because the knee follows memory bandwidth rather than compute.

MoE routing imbalance (measured). The ratio of grouped-GEMM latency under a skewed expert distribution to the same shape under a balanced one, as the median and 90th percentile over many paired shapes. Not a curve fit, so fitted: false.

Descriptor figures (vendor_spec). HBM derate and latency, the host-link bandwidth, peer-to-peer latency, NCCL communicator buffer sizes and the engine's non-weight workspace, transcribed from AISimulate's systems/<sku>.yaml.

Not every family here is read by the kernel today; the reference overview lists which. A100-80 and A100-SXM are the same silicon, so their entries share one scope.

docs.title: cost-model-recurrent
docs.text:
The constants for recurrent (linear-attention) state updates in hybrid models, priced like the other primitives as a floor plus a rate:

latency = recurrent_decode_floor_<kind> + tokens / recurrent_decode_rate_<kind>

Three kinds are fitted: KDA (Kimi-K3), GDN, and Mamba2 (Nemotron-3).

Coverage differs by kind, and it matters more than the values. The KDA sweep covers the whole layer. The Mamba2 sweep covers only the convolution; the selective scan that makes up the rest of a Mamba2 layer is in no AISimulate collection. The Mamba2 entries are therefore a lower bound on a Mamba2 layer's cost, and their rationale says so.

The geometry is part of the fit. These constants carry no head-count term, so each is fitted at the head geometry the catalog's model declares. Pooling geometries fits none of them.

L40S is deliberately absent: its fits are markedly worse than on every other part, and the set's header records the figures.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Three documents record how the registry's numbers are obtained and checked. They are written for someone who wants to challenge a value: each claim comes with the measurement behind it, and the claims later found wrong are kept, marked as retracted, next to what replaced them.

Methodology The rules: what a coefficient is, which dataset may be used for what, how fits are held out, and the record of each decision made under those rules. Reproducing the coefficients The mechanics: where the data is, and which command regenerates which family. Choosing the overlap band One model-selection decision, worked through: which of the kernel's two step-time estimates a consumer should use.

docs.title: The argument in brief
docs.text:
1. A coefficient is a constant of a law the kernel evaluates, never a per-model correction. Its value and its citation move together. §1
  2. Fit the engine you predict. AISimulate measures several engines; the right lane is decided per operator, by evidence. §2
  3. Each dataset has one job. Operator sweeps fit; whole-forward measurements validate and select; end-to-end runs only evaluate. A whole-pass total cannot identify a per-primitive constant. §3
  4. Hold out along a dimension that generalization must cross: a part, a model, a parallelism, a shape axis. Never a random row split. §4, §7
  5. A better fit to one primitive can be a worse model. Nothing ships without an end-to-end check. §3
  6. Gaps are declared. An assumed value says what it rests on and what would replace it. §6.0

docs.title: Where to look for a specific question
docs.text: Question Section Why is this family on this engine's measurements? §2, §8 Which values can be reproduced, and which cannot? §6.0 How do I reproduce an accuracy figure exactly? §6.1 Why is a part missing from a family? §5 How are 8- and 16-rank collectives priced on parts never swept at those widths? §8.5 What did the whole-forward data find? §9 Why does sparse MLA have no rate of its own? §10 How do the memory terms compose? §11

docs.title: Reading the numbers in these documents
docs.text: The methodology is a record kept as the work proceeded, and its tables give the counts and figures measured when each section was written. Counts of entries move with every refit. For the registry as it stands, use the reference pages, which are generated from the data on every build. Where the two disagree on a count, the reference pages are current.

docs.title: Using the registry
docs.text: The registry is read from disk, by path, at run time. Nothing is installed and nothing is fetched over the network: a consumer is given the root of a clone and opens coefficients/<set>.yaml beneath it.

docs.title: Get a copy
docs.text:
Clone a release, not main. A release fixes every value, and an estimate is reproducible only if the coefficients behind it are.

git clone --branch v0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git

v0.3.0 is the newest release at the time this page was built. Releases and pinning explains what a version number does and does not promise.

docs.title: Run BLIS with it
docs.text:
The simulator prices steps through blis-latency-kernel when run with --latency-model blis-latency-kernel. That path is on the kernel-exclusive branch of the sriumcp/inference-sim fork, open as inference-sim#1851. It reads the deployment from a scenario file, the model and hardware from a catalog clone, and the coefficients from a registry clone:

./blis run --latency-model blis-latency-kernel \
    --scenarios path/to/scenarios --scenario kimi-k3-h100-nospec.yaml \
    --catalog path/to/blis-catalog \
    --registry path/to/blis-registry

The scenario's coefficients: list names the sets to load, and its cluster.hardware selects the entries that apply. --registry is required on this path; the run stops with an error rather than fall back to other coefficients.

docs.title: Use it from Go
docs.text:
blis-latency-kernel resolves a scenario file against the three roots and returns a kernel ready to price steps:

import latencykernel "github.com/inference-sim/blis-latency-kernel"

k, err := latencykernel.Open("kimi-k3-h100-nospec.yaml", latencykernel.Repos{
    Scenarios: "path/to/scenarios",
    Catalog:   "path/to/blis-catalog",
    Registry:  "path/to/blis-registry",
})

To read one set without the kernel, load and validate it with blis-schemas, as the kernel does:

import blisschemas "github.com/inference-sim/blis-schemas"

set, err := blisschemas.LoadCoefficientSet("path/to/blis-registry/coefficients/cost-model-attention.yaml")
if err != nil {
    return err // unreadable, or an unknown field
}
if p := set.Validate(); !p.OK() {
    return p // every finding, each naming the entry it is about
}
for _, e := range set.Coefficients {
    fmt.Println(e.Name, e.Scope.Hardware, e.Value, e.Units, e.Method)
}

docs.title: Read it from anything else
docs.text:
The files are plain YAML. Each item in coefficients is a map with a single key, the coefficient's name:

import yaml

with open("coefficients/cost-model-attention.yaml") as f:
    doc = yaml.safe_load(f)

for item in doc["coefficients"]:
    (name, entry), = item.items()
    print(name, entry["scope"]["hardware"], entry["value"], entry["units"], entry["method"])

A name can occur more than once in a set, once per scope. A reader that builds a dictionary keyed by name alone will keep one part's value and silently drop the rest. Key by name and scope, or filter by scope first, as the kernel does.

docs.title: Check where a number came from
docs.text: Every value in the coefficient set reference links to its entry in the committed file at the revision the page was built from. The entry carries the citation, the rationale and the scope. Follow the citation to the dataset; the reproduction guide gives the command that regenerates it.

docs.title: Releases and pinning
docs.text: A release is a git tag, vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, on main, with a GitHub release that describes what changed. It fixes every value in every set. A consumer that records which release it read can reproduce its coefficients exactly.

docs.title: Pin the exact tag
docs.text:
The version number orders releases. It does not promise that values are unchanged between them: refitting a family, adding a part and adding a set all change what a scenario resolves to, and each is a normal reason to release, at any of the three levels. Pin the full tag, and record it next to any figure computed with it.

git clone --branch v0.3.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/inference-sim/blis-registry.git

To see what moved between two releases, compare them:

git diff v0.1.0 v0.1.1 --stat -- coefficients/

The releases page summarizes each one and links the pull requests behind it.

docs.title: Versions of this site
docs.text:
The documentation is published once per release, so the reference pages always show the numbers of the version being read.

In the version selector Built from Updated X.Y.Z the release tag vX.Y.Z when the release is published latest the highest release moves to each new highest release dev (main) main on every merge

The site's root opens latest. Every other version shows a banner saying it is not the newest release. Versions are full release numbers, not X.Y, because a patch release can change values, and each release's pages must show that release's values.
